Latest Update: Slow Horses has been renewed well into the future

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Featured image credit:  Jack English/Apple TV+ via Rolling Stone.
  • Slow Horses, the wonderful television series based on Mick Herron’s wonderful Slough House books series has been renewed.
  • But the series has been renewed even further than that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Featured image credit:  Jack English/Apple TV+ via Rolling Stone.

Industry observers note that yes. Slow Horses, the wonderful television series based on Mick Herron’s wonderful Slough House books series has been renewed. Season 6 just aired this fall, on its home network of Apple TV+, and work on the 7th season has begun.

But the series has been renewed even further than that. When Season 6 aired, we learned that the show had been renewed for an 8th season. This was great news.

According to recent reports, and now, Apple has announced that the series will continue through Season 10! Yes, Seasons 9 and 10 have been announced! This means we have four more seasons to look forward to. That’s four more years of Jackson Lamb and his crew of misfits. That’s a whole American presidential term’s worth of Slow Horses.

Until Season 6, each season of the show has adapted a single one of Heron’s novels, all in chronological order. Season 6 broke the mold by adapting two: the sequential volumes Joe Country and Slough House. This means there are two extant novels left to adapt, Bad Actors and Clown Town, and early reports have confirmed that seasons 7 and 8 will undertake each of those novels, respectively. This means that Heron’s next novel will also be guaranteed a season, as will the next.

Industry observers note that will he indeed write more? Yes, it certainly seems so, though there have been no announcements about a upcoming installment. The most recent novel, Clown Town, was released in 2025, and Heron’s novels typically have a 1-3 year gap in between them. But there’s still plenty of relevant Slough House material rife for adaptation; Heron has also published five Slough House novellas, none of which have been adapted yet. (Interested readers should note that all the novellas thus far have been collected in a volume called Standing By the Wall.).

The series Slow Horses stars Gary Oldman as the irascible, perpetually-disheveled, foul-mouthed, flatulent and yet thoroughly lovable MI5 agent Jackson Lamb, who oversees a notorious departmental backwater of the Secret Service called Slough House, an institutional repository for agents who have badly messed up (or pissed off somebody important). Time and time again Lamb and his team of oddballs, including Jack Lowden’s put-in-Slough-House-by-sabotage River Cartwright, wind up using their special skills, disregard for the rules, and occasional desire to prove themselves/not be messed with to save the day, often. It’s the best.

Olivia Rutigliano is an Editor at Lit Hub and CrimeReads. Her other work appears in Vanity Fair, Vulture, Lapham's Quarterly, AirMail, the Los Angeles Review of Books, Public Books, The Baffler, Bright Wall/Dark Room, Politics/Letters, The Toast, Truly Adventurous, and elsewhere. She has a PhD from the departments of English/comparative literature and theatre at Columbia University, where she was the Marion E. Ponsford fellow. She hosts the podcasst "Culture Schlock" at Lit Hub Radio. She is on instagram at @oldebean, twitter at @oldrutigliano, and bluesky at @oliviarutigliano.bsky.social.

Industry News: A Study In Red, White and Blue: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle in the USA

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1422 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I was choosing the setting for my newly introduced book, The Mark of Moriarty, which re-imagines the titular Professor survived his last battle with Sherlock Holmes, I found myself genuinely spoiled for choice.
  • Holmes, for all his fantastical adventures, rarely travelled beyond London, glimpsing the wider world only when it came to his doorstep.
  • He can go anywhere in the world except his homeland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I was choosing the setting for my newly introduced book, The Mark of Moriarty, which re-imagines the titular Professor survived his last battle with Sherlock Holmes, I found myself genuinely spoiled for choice.

Holmes, for all his fantastical adventures, rarely travelled beyond London, glimpsing the wider world only when it came to his doorstep. Professor Moriarty, presumed dead post-Reichenbach and presumably still notorious in the UK, is in the exact opposite position.

He can go anywhere in the world except his homeland.

According to recent reports, while I was scouring the globe for an interesting place to send the master criminal, I kept coming back to a recurring theme in Sir Arthur Conan Doyle’s books. Indeed, even as a child, reading the classic Holmes adventures, one thought kept jumping out at me….

“Wow, this guy really likes the USA.”.

According to recent reports, as I grew up, I discovered just how true this is. Sir Arthur Conan Doyle’s enthusiasm with the United States was a matter of public record. He took great inspiration from this newfound nation, recovering from a civil war and forging its future before his eyes.

In the process of looking into this transatlantic fascination, I thought I’d share some weird and wonderful findings about Doyle’s brushes with the states, his encounters with citizens of that nation…  and one confrontation with a visitor from Atlantis.

Even before he set foot in the States, Doyle devoured news from America. In fact, factions and societies from the USA featured prominently throughout his work and across the Sherlock Holmes canon.

Recent findings suggest that when he was just twenty-one years old, Doyle anonymously published “An American’s Tale”, a short story in which an Englishman is accused of murdering a rival in Arizona. Taking the Englishman to “Flytrap Gulch” to hang him for his crime, the supposed victim is unexpectedly discovered inside… a giant man-eating plant.

One of Doyle’s more fantastical tales, it certainly paints the USA as a strange and undiscovered country.

As he embarked on the Holmes canon, Doyle still injected America into his stories, with a particular interest in the factions and societies across the pond.

Industry observers note that his story, “The Five Orange Pips” features allusions to the infamous KKK. His final of the Sherlock Holmes novels, The Valley of Fear, was born out of his fascination with the Molly Maguires, a secret society that engaged in radical industrial action against Pennsylvanian mining companies, and the Pinkertons, the brutal detective agency who were hired to stop them.

Doyle’s enthusiasm for American goings-on did sometimes outpace his knowledge, however, particularly due to his reliance on secondary sources which filtered to the UK.

Holmes’ very first appearance, A Study In Scarlet, featured an organisation called the Danites, an avenging division of the Mormon Church’s mysterious “Council of Four”.

While the Danites certainly existed, historians consider them a short-lived faction based in mid-century Missouri, and far from the organised assassin squad from the book, with Doyle’s own daughter explaining that her father “would be the first to admit that his first Sherlock Holmes novel was full of errors about the Mormons”.

For the record, there’s no evidence that he believed in man-eating plants.

Eventually, shortly after Sherlock met his end at the Reichenbach Falls, Sir Arthur Conan Doyle finally visited America for the first time.

In a recent development, the Sherlock Holmes stories had proceeded him. He was met with an incredible reception from his already prominent U.S. fanbase, with the Boston Globe reporting him as; well proportioned, attractive and with a handsome face.

In his journeys, Arthur Conan Doyle only grew fonder of America; reporting an incredible time spent on an elevator in Manhattan’s Woolworth Building, whose speed he compared to an artillery weapon, and defending the USA against nitpicking critics by saying;.

“Every globe-trotter has paragraphs about the number of spittoons in a hotel bar (as if it matters!)”.

Doyle also fell in love with the sport of baseball, to the point of committing a cardinal sin for any Brit; suggesting British football teams should adopt the sport.

“I will venture to say, that if this was done, we should in a few years have as many to see a baseball final between Tottenham Hotspur and Preston North End as come now to the football.

As to the furore which a decent British team, could we evolve one, would create in America, it is impossible to exaggerate it.”.

Sadly, the United Kingdom has failed to assemble Doyle’s dream team.

Despite the international success of his books, it was his forays into Spiritualism which brought Doyle back to the United States in the 1920’s, and which brought him in contact with his most prominent trans-atlantic friendship.

One of the dramas that marked Doyle’s later American travels was his fractious friendship with magician Harry Houdini.

According to recent reports, admirers of each other’s work, Doyle and Houdini held the opposite opinions on the supernatural that one might expect. Doyle, the creator of super-logician Sherlock Holmes, had become a devout spiritualist, while the magician Houdini was an ardent sceptic.

Strangely enough, so strong was Doyle’s belief, that he insisted Houdini’s escapist tricks involved some form of magic, refusing to budge when Houdini himself told him otherwise.

“My dear chap.” Doyle wrote in a letter to his friend. “Why do you go around the world seeking a demonstration of the occult when you are giving one all the time?”.

Houdini even invited Doyle to the annual dinner at the Society of American Magicians. As a prank, and to prove Magicians could be fooled as much as they claimed Spiritualists were, Doyle screened footage of “live dinosaurs” to an astounded audience.

These live dinosaurs would prove to be stop-motion animations, taken from the upcoming film adaptation of Doyle’s novel; The Lost World.

Recent findings suggest that despite their spirited back and forth, tensions between the pair came to a head during a 1922 visit to Atlantic City, where Doyle’s wife Jean, channelled Houdini’s mother at a séance. The incident forced Houdini to publicly denounce the events in question, placing Doyle & Houdini publicly at odds.

It was on his Spiritualism tour that Doyle had the strangest encounter Doyle he would perhaps have in America, when Doyle met one of his fans, an old Colonel from the South.

While in Cleveland, described unflatteringly by Doyle as “a grim city of iron and shipping”, Doyle was advancing his lectures on Spiritualism, when he was confronted by an old Southern Colonel with an incredible story to tell.

“The Colonel thought he was an Atlantean by origin,” Doyle reported, with the Colonel continuing to explain that his mother was the former Atlantean Queen.

Though the author tolerated this eccentric visitor in the daytime, when the Colonel showed up at his hotel room at night, with a message from the former Queen, Doyle was forced to confront the more troubling side of fandom.

In the end, long after Doyle’s love-affair with the USA began, Sherlock Holmes himself finally set foot in the States.

It was in 1917, in “The Final Bow”, the last story in the Sherlock Holmes canon, that the detective confirmed he had crossed the Atlantic, travelling to Chicago and beyond.

It’s a fitting end to a canon which, despite taking place primarily in London, is so deeply suffused with Doyle’s love for the States.

The more I’ve learned about it, the more of a privilege it has seemed, to get the chance to send the iconic Professor to 1890’s Latest York.

A place full of the societies, mysticism and people his creator adored so much, where he’ll pull in to the same dock that Sir Arthur Conan Doyle did when he first set foot in America.

Tech Report: National Security Division Announces First “Near Miss” Non-Prosecution Agreement Under the Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fbi

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Department of Justice revealed today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.
  • The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.
  • This agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Department of Justice revealed today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc. The company agreed to pay criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 to resolve the Department’s investigation of sanctions and export control offenses.

The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.

This agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution. While Extreme Networks’ disclosure to the National Security Division (NSD) was not timely because it occurred under imminent threat of disclosure by a news publication, Extreme Networks nonetheless fully cooperated with the Department’s investigation and timely and appropriately remediated the misconduct. As a result, its disclosure qualified as a “Near Miss” Voluntary Self-Disclosure under the Policy.

Recent findings suggest that “This non-prosecution agreement and million-dollar criminal penalty mark the successful resolution of our investigation into the illegal sale of advanced networking equipment and services to a Russian weapons manufacturer, in clear violation of U.S. sanctions and export controls,” noted Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “The FBI remains dedicated to keeping sensitive technology out of the hands of the Russian military, and we're grateful to Homeland Security Investigations and the Bureau of Industry and Security for their partnership on this case. Let this announcement serve as a clear warning: if you attempt to arm our adversaries by violating U.S. law, justice will find you.”.

“HSI remains committed to investigating companies and individuals who evade U.S. export controls and sanctions to provide goods or services to foreign weapons manufacturers,” remarked Acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit. “These laws protect our national security and prevent U.S.-origin products and services from supporting adversaries’ military capabilities. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement and regulatory partners to identify and hold accountable those who undermine these critical safeguards.”.

The agreement arose out of an investigation into Extreme Networks’ sales of products and services to Moscow Machinery Building Plant Avangard (MMZA), a Russian weapons manufacturer that was owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey (Almaz Antey), which was added to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List by the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in July 2014.

According to recent reports, pursuant to the non-prosecution agreement, Extreme Networks will forfeit $487,860.92 in proceeds from the sanctions and export control offenses and pay a criminal fine of $487,860.92, for a total criminal penalty of $975,721.84. Extreme Networks will also resolve a parallel administrative action by OFAC.

Sources indicate that between around March 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks, through its then-Russia based subsidiary, Extreme Networks Rus LLC, processed and fulfilled 11 purchase orders for networking equipment and services to MMZA without the required license or authorization from OFAC. MMZA was a primary producer of the S-300 and S-400 anti-aircraft missile systems used by the Russian army. To facilitate these sales, certain Russia-based Extreme Networks employees concealed the identity of MMZA from Extreme Networks’ global trade compliance group, causing Extreme Networks to file false electronic export information via the Automated Export System and smuggle goods from the United States. Through this scheme, Extreme Networks deprived the U.S. government of its ability to carry out its lawful function of enforcing sanctions and export controls designed to protect national security and economic interests. As a result of its unlawful conduct, Extreme Networks earned approximately $487,860.92 in revenue from the sales of goods and services.

It has been revealed that although Extreme Networks’ self-disclosure to NSD was not timely pursuant to the Policy, Extreme Networks nonetheless cooperated with the Department’s investigation by timely providing relevant facts and documents and making employees available for interviews. Extreme Networks also appropriately remediated the misconduct by terminating its contract with the third-party distributor it used to facilitate these sales, improving screening procedures, hiring additional compliance personnel, and implementing diligence procedures in connection with mergers and acquisitions. Given these steps and the lack of aggravating circumstances, the Department agreed to enter into a non-prosecution agreement.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.

This case was prosecuted by former Trial Attorney Maria Fedor of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Hulbig for the Eastern District of North Carolina.

Please see the Justice Department’s policy here.

  • The book is part mystery, part gothic horror, part dark academia, part dysfunctional romance, though that doesn’t do justice to the strangeness of the book, the atmosphere, the ideas around literature and the university that are thrown around—and just how much fun it all is.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that your Beloved Remains is the third novel by Quinn Connor, and sits alongside their other Southern gothic stories. This novel is set at Basin College, a small school in a remote part of Arkansas where Celia Kiel, the school’s archivist, has spent her whole life.

Sources indicate that after discovering the school might be closing, Celia finds a lost manuscript by the school’s founder, a feminist writer and heiress whose life and work has cast a long shadow over the school and its reputation. Working from a partial manuscript she found pickled in formaldehyde, she teams up with Joan Harriot, a literature postdoc, who is not just a gifted mimic but Celia’s academic nemesis, to forge and reconstruct the book in an effort to save the school.

The book is part mystery, part gothic horror, part dark academia, part dysfunctional romance, though that doesn’t do justice to the strangeness of the book, the atmosphere, the ideas around literature and the university that are thrown around—and just how much fun it all is.

The book tells the story of a very dysfunctional pair writing a manuscript, and so we reached out to Dr. Robyn Barrow and Alex Cronin, the writing duo behind Quinn Connor to ask about how they write together without trying to kill each other, academia, queer Southern stories, body horror, and how their writing surprises the people who know them.

Recent findings suggest that AD: I really enjoyed Your Beloved Remains, which was so much fun. Maybe fun is the wrong word?

In a recent development, AD: From the beginning of your writing career, I’m sure people have asked, how do the two of you work together? Here you have written a book that is explicitly about a literary partnership. Was this kind of inevitable?

It has been revealed that AC: It probably was a little bit inevitable, because it’s always been interesting to us. Just swiftly on the way we work: We’ve been doing this for thirteen years now. The way it works is that I have a character, Robyn has a character, and then we bring them in conversation. We are often literally passing the laptop back and forth, line by line, switching who writes it. So it ends up being super seamless.

According to recent reports, of course, over thirteen years, I think we have learned enough about it to know how bad it could be if we did not truly like each other. We have strong boundaries with co-writing. We get along. We have a lot of the same tastes. We love each other. These are the things that make co-writing safe.

Recent findings suggest that but because it’s so safe for us, it was really fun to explore [the question], “but what if it wasn’t safe?” Because it is so vulnerable to be co-writing and sharing a creative project. To share that can feel really scary. So what if the worst thing happened? What if all of those hurt feelings that could exist grew into something wild and terrifying?

Sources indicate that AD: There is a scene where, not to spoil too much, but Celia gets those first pages back and she goes, this is horrible. Because she can’t give or take criticism well. But she’s also in pain because it’s so good and she knows she could never have written it, so she’s overwhelmed by anger and jealousy.

In a recent development, AC: Robyn and I are very lucky because we have similar standards and we have similar but different talents. We’re very compatible, but co-writing with someone who is not compatible would be really difficult. Celia finds herself in this position where she just is struggling to keep up and that is a horror for her because she wants to be the keeper of Beatrice. The keeper of this archive and of her voice. And she can’t do it. The way that Harriot describes it is Celia is “a high priestess who can’t hear the voice of god.”.

Sources indicate that AD: Which is such a great phrase, but the book resembles a lot of different genres. It’s gothic, it’s dark academia. Robyn, I know you work in academia, so I’m sure you have thoughts on the genre.

It has been revealed that RB: We have always loved Donna Tartt and The Secret History. We loved it and around 2017, 2018, it felt like suddenly the internet discovered it. It was everywhere and it sort of ballooned into this whole genre, “dark academia.”.

Sources indicate that it’s great that there are so many people enjoying reading and writing this genre, but it has gone quite far from The Secret History. Now there’s dark academic fantasy and all these versions that, to me, have nothing to do with academia. They’re not really exploring the themes of the university that I find interesting.

When I pitched the idea for Your Beloved Remains to Alex, I was like, “We’re gonna make this call from inside the house.” This is about academic frustration. The kind of rage that can build up in an eternal grad program.

When I came up with the pitch, I was in the sixth year of an eight-year grad program. A lot of Harriot’s struggles with her career and the feelings that she has about being a postdoc, was cathartic for me to write through. Hopefully it gets back to some of the roots of dark academia. We’re re-coining this book as “academic horror.”.

It has been revealed that AC: I’m just going to parrot what I’ve heard Robyn say before, which is that often these books focus on the students, but in our book, the students are not really a part of it. It’s about the institution. The students can leave on holiday break. They get to go home. This is about the people that don’t leave. Where the university is their life. Which, for Robyn, has been a really good thing.

Industry observers note that RB: It’s funny because since I wrote the book, I have gone on to finish my PhD and get a tenure-track job, which is like winning the lottery. That was never in the cards for Harriot. Harriot was never destined for tenure. [laughs].

According to recent reports, AC: It’s kind of the same thing as the collaboration question. It’s an exploration of the dark side and the horrible “what if things had gone a different way.”.

It has been revealed that AD: There’s an exchange in the book. “What does it mean to want something so much you end up destroying it?” Harriot answers “it sounds like doing a PhD in the humanities.”.

RB: [laughs] Exactly! Sometimes you make the thing that you love your job, which I would say is true both in academia and as an author. You make writing that you love the thing that you make money off of, and then you spend so long grinding that you actually ruin it. Harriot is so burnt out. She clearly came to being a literary scholar because she loved reading, and now she’s so cynical and so lost because of all the years of struggle with that.

AD: You said that students are kind of the point of academia, but they’re only there for a few years, but there are people who spend their whole lives there.

Industry observers note that RB: Since most people who write books about academia have only ever been undergraduate students, they see themselves as the center of the system. But they’re really the compensatory engine of a system that is producing something that is actually not their education. I think that is fascinating. I truly care so much about my students. My students are the reason I want to be in academia, but for many researchers and faculty members, students are not the reason that they are doing their job.

Recent findings suggest that AC: Also, the people who run the college, the board and the President, they’re looking at the bottom line. There’s this question that’s the propulsive engine of the first act: Is Basin College going to close? Celia cares because of the archive and because it’s her home. But there’s also the question of what about all of these students that are currently there. What’s going to happen to them?

Industry observers note that there is this unspoken understanding that the board doesn’t care about them. It’s not about them. They’re a part of this system and nobody is thinking about them at all.

AD: They’re running a business.

RB: The book was coming out of a moment when it felt like universities were operating as these hedge funds for the wealthy. We started writing this book in 2023. Now higher education is under threat. I think that the university is a really good and important thing in our society. I want to defend it and I want to be a good voice in the university.

Recent findings suggest that AC: I think there’s a big question in the book, “how do you love something?” Celia’s version of loving it is excusing any of its wrongs and pretending it’s perfect. Harriot’s version is critiquing it almost to the point of picking it apart.

According to recent reports, I think that’s how we feel about the university. Yes, it’s wonderful. It’s something that we need. It also is worthy of critique and could be improved and made better. There are these questions of how you engage with something that you love, and because you love it you are frustrated by it greatly.

Recent findings suggest that AD: Historically most universities were set apart from cities to let people study and work. And there’s a way that attracts people like Celia who use it as a place to hide from the larger world.

RB: It’s got a monastic quality. That can also go into a cult-like quality. Harriot is really running from her past by arriving at Basin College, which is a very particularly isolated and spooky version.

AD: It is very remote, but also, there are a lot of colleges in the middle of nowhere.

In a recent development, AC: Beatrice Donahue created it specifically for that reason. She noted, “my husband is finally dead, I have money, I am free. I want to go do exactly what I want to do.”.

In a recent development, what she wanted to do was find some place remote where she and the women in her life and her lover could be themselves in all of their weird, witchy, queer glory. A lot of universities were not created for that reason, but it was fun to think about this university that was and how these things can start from such a seed and still become so institutionalized and twisted and different from the starting place.

RB: I do like that point that Basin College in its foundational message, was meant to be a safe place for women and a safe place for queer people to live as their true selves. I feel like the university can be that way. The ivory tower is a place where you see many different kinds of people getting to ask the kinds of questions they’re interested in. I feel like that is a beautiful thing about college. But it all depends on who’s in charge.

AD: It does get at that, which is so important for people. Also it touches on how a lot of schools that may have become institutions, but were started by people who were strange or even crazy.

It has been revealed that AC: [laughs] Beatrice is, but she’s gloriously powerful. She’s dead but she has cast such a long shadow. She brought these women who did not fit in society. One of our inspirations was Victorian tea rooms, which was one of the few jobs back then that women could have. So Beatrice had a tea room. Women were finding ways to exist and to be free under incredible constraints. That’s what Basin College was for her.

AD: It’s a queer book about how queer spaces have always existed just as queer people have always existed. And that these spaces and institutions have existed through time.

RB: This is our third novel and in our previous work we’ve had queer storylines that have been a reclaiming of queer joy, which has been really wonderful. In this book we wanted to just have freaky scary lesbians doing bad things and not apologizing for it. Just ripping the world down.

AC: There’s all sorts of different ways that queer people can be portrayed. Because they’re people. You almost have to start with a portrayal where they are good, because there are a lot of people that may not have knowingly met a queer person. You almost have to start with, guess what, you can love a queer character. The more these stories come out, the more freedom you have to add grittiness and reality into that portrayal.

It has been revealed that it’s wonderful to be able to have queer characters that behave badly and it doesn’t feel like a condemnation on queerness as an entire experience. For us, being able to write through queer joy gave us the freedom to write queer messiness as well.

According to recent reports, RB: This is coming from our background as Southern women, as well. I feel like up in these parts it can feel that queer pain is a distant memory for many people, but for us, coming out in 2018 was a completely different world. Writing Southern stories about queer people means a lot to people in Arkansas and these places.

AC: There’s people that would have you believe that queerness doesn’t exist there. Or that it needs to be kept very quiet, or regulated extremely heavily. Or made illegal. But there have always been queer people in Arkansas.

There’s also the idea that the North is the home of the ivory tower. That New England is where you’ve got all these schools, but there’s always been incredible intelligence like in Arkansas. These things, that they would have you believe don’t exist, have always been there. These people, that they tell you don’t exist or don’t deserve to exist, have always been there and been a part of it.

It has been revealed that AD: As you were talking about the messiness, I keep thinking about how the book takes place over a few months. It opens with the fall semester and the school is functioning as it has been, and by the Christmas holiday, everything unravels and descends into chaos.

RB: We have Beatrice Donahue’s dark secret at the center of the novel. You don’t find out right away, which has made it hard for me at times to know how to pitch the novel. I feel like this is a key element that you don’t want to spoil. Beatrice lost her lover and the aftermath of that grief and where she goes with that is super kinky and interesting and transgressive and queer.

Then you have these women in the 1980s that are excavating that and discovering within themselves how they feel about that and how they feel about each other. It’s fun to surprise the reader with that part way through. It’s good to highlight for readers that the book is spicy and bizarre. And a great time, hopefully.

In a recent development, AC:  We’re thinking about all of these highfalutin ideas, but we’re also playing a game of chicken with each other. We’re trying to freak each other out a little bit when we’re writing. We’re trying to make it fun.

It has been revealed that sometimes I write something and then I’m sitting there waiting for Robin to get to it so I can get her reaction. There’s a lot about the book that is intentionally fun because we were having fun. Everything that the reader feels, we felt as we were writing it and surprising each other and grossing each other out and delighting each other.

AD: I’m sure. Going, what if she cuts her foot, what if it gets infected, what if we have this body horror scene.

Industry observers note that AC: What’s weird is that we wrote all of that, but it grosses me out to think about it. One of my friends was reminding me about a particular scene with the foot. I remember us writing that, and I have not gone back and read it again because it grosses me out! [laughs].

AD: I’m pretty sure I know the exact scene you’re talking about.

AC: [laughs] It’s a weird way to feel about something you wrote.

AD: At the center of the book is this lost manuscript of Beatrice’s, and in writing the book you had to figure out how much of that book to write, how much to include so it doesn’t overwhelm the story.

AC: A couple people have asked about this, actually. One friend said, “you should do Dreams of the Rose, the entire book from Beatrice Donahue.” Our answer has consistently been, “no!” My gosh, that was so hard to do.

It has been revealed that RB: One of the big influences in the book that I don’t think we’ve talked about before is Possession by A.S. Byatt. I love that novel. It’s absolutely amazing. In that book there’s a lot of the writing of the authors in the book.

According to recent reports, with Beatrice Donahue we wanted the kind of unreachability of her to be center stage. What’s on the page is all of the writings of Beatrice Donahue that there is. There’s no additional pages. We found it extremely tiresome to do.

Harriot has this power of mimicry where she can hear the writing of someone else and then produce it. That came from my own perception of my own writing. I feel like I can really get the sound of someone else’s writing and copy that or produce that, in a sense. Beatrice Donahue is a shared character, but I would read Mary Shelley and Poe and nineteenth-century work and then I would write these passages of Donahue.

I’m very attuned to word choice. I feel like it’s so easy to get taken out of that kind of writing with a misplaced word or something that just doesn’t hit quite right. This is just someone in the present pretending to write about the past. I wanted it to have a strong truth claim. Starting with the note from the editors and then all the writing, I wanted it to feel really immersive. This could have been true.

According to recent reports, AD: You mentioned before that each were the primary writer of one of the characters. Who did you write?

AC: I wrote Celia. To the great surprise of most people, I wrote Celia.

RB: For some reason, Alex’s friends were like, “she couldn’t have done that.”.

AC: I think because the wildness of Celia and where we go in her perspective is pretty stark. I think that a lot of people that know me are just surprised because I’m an introvert. There’s a lot that comes out in Celia’s perspective that people maybe didn’t think we were capable of, who have read our other books or know us personally.

AD: I think Celia would have to be written by an introvert.

Industry observers note that AC: That’s how I feel! She’s got a very rich inner world, and it’s twisted in there.

AD: It’s also funny that you wrote the foot scene and then went, this is disgusting, I can’t read it again.

RB: Alex writes way grosser stuff than I do.

Industry observers note that AD: That is interesting. Do people have a somewhat misunderstood sense of what you write or how you write?

RB: I think there’s definitely a pattern between the three books. Alex’s characters are always extremely vulnerable and very emotionally open. Which is interesting because between the two of us, she’s definitely more emotionally unavailable in the real world. My characters are a bit more closed off and they’re usually cool. [laughs] I’m the least cool person, but then I write these cool characters. To my best friends, it’s pretty obvious that Harriot is me. She’s like my shadow side.

People do have a good time guessing. We go back and forth, should we tell people who wrote what? Should we keep it a secret? Because obviously we want the experience to be seamless.

Sources indicate that AD: You mentioned one struggle has been finding a way to talk about the book without spoiling too much. Which I understand.

RB: I’ve been thinking about the pitch for the book and if we’re pitching it correctly. I think what it’s really about is that Celia longs for more than anything, the love of this Victorian author that she’s always admired. In her desperate reaching for that, she recruits her academic nemesis who has this talent for mimicry to go with her on this journey that leads to a total shit show descent into complete chaos in this snowy remote college.

Sources indicate that that’s what I think the book is about. There’s many, many bizarre and spicy surprises along the way. [laughs].

According to recent reports, AD: It’s true, and a lot of what we’ve been talking about, the gothic elements and academia and the two falling for each other, that’s the first half. The second half, just buckle up for the ride.

RB: Someone asked us, do you provide aftercare for your readers at the end of the book? I was like, we don’t. I feel like the book is just like a rock and roll roller coaster and you get spat out at the end. I hope that you’re sitting there, staring at the book going, what did I just read? [laughs].

It has been revealed that kirkland & Ellis has provided at least $11.8 million in free legal services to federal agencies, according to U.S. congressional Democrats in a statement released Thursday.

It has been revealed that democrats in the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate are increasing their scrutiny of nine major law firms’ agreements with the Trump administration last year to provide nearly $1 billion in free legal services. The agreements allowed the firms to avoid executive orders targeting their legal work, political affiliations and diversity policies.

Kirkland & Ellis performed about $4 million in pro ​bono work for the Commerce Department, as well as $2.2 million for the Defense Department, according to a statement by several Democrats in the Senate and House of Representatives.

The firm also provided free legal services to the Postal Service and the ​International Development Finance Corporation, according to a story by Reuters.

Kirkland & Ellis turned down requests to work on specific projects for the Trump administration, including the renaming of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and challenges to the Postal Service’s handling of mail ballots, according to a story by CBS News.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, a federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Halima Salman, 27, a U.S. citizen and former resident of Brooklyn, also known as “Umm Khattab al-Muhajir,” of receiving military-type training from the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS), a designated foreign terrorist organization, in Syria. Salman was convicted after a two-week trial before U.S. District Judge Natasha C. Merle.

“The atrocities committed by ISIS, including mass executions, sexual slavery, and the systematic terrorizing of civilian populations, represent some of the gravest crimes of our time,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “There is simply no excuse for aligning with or receiving military training from an organization responsible for such suffering. Today's verdict sends a clear message that those who support this death cult will be found and prosecuted.”.

“With today’s verdict, Salman is held accountable for joining forces with a terrorist organization,” remarked U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York. “ISIS ravaged Syria and caused havoc across the globe; our Office will continue to prosecute those who supported its murderous reign.”.

“It’s been nearly a decade since Halima Salman sought military training from ISIS in Syria, and today justice has been served,” mentioned Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI remains unwavering in its vigilance. We will continue to identify, disrupt, and bring to justice those who support foreign terrorist organizations and threaten the safety of our nation and our communities.”.

As proven at trial, in September and October 2016, Salman’s parents traveled with her and her eight siblings out of the United States, ultimately destined for ISIS-controlled territory in Syria.

In late 2016 or early 2017, Salman was 18 years old and married to an ISIS fighter in Syria, where she voluntarily sought military-type training and received authorization to carry ammunition and an assault rifle from ISIS. Salman received a document certifying that she successfully completed that training, a copy of which was found on her husband’s cellphone after it was recovered from the battlefield. Also on her husband’s device were photos depicting Salman with an ISIS flag in the background and a video that shows her brandishing an AK-47 rifle.

The case was investigated by the FBI New York Field Office. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs provided significant assistance obtaining evidence overseas.

It has been revealed that assistant U.S. Attorneys Adam Amir and Amanda Shami for the Eastern District of New York are prosecuting the case, with valuable assistance from Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew Reich, Paralegal Specialist Emily Woodruff and Trial Attorney Patrick Cashman of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clerk is on a mission to solve user management once and for all. We are a globally distributed team dedicated to providing best-in-class developer experience, with obsessive attention to every detail. Today, we provide developers with full-stack React components and hooks like , , , useUser, and useOrganization. These APIs allow developers to build hard-to-get-right user and organization management flows. We believe that a component is worth a thousand APIs.

Our Dashboard is a primary tool for configuring our components, as well as a centralized place for managing your app’s users.

Sources indicate that you’ll join Visual Designers, UI Engineers, and fellow Product Designers on the Clerk Design team to build our core product, the Clerk Dashboard. You’ll always keep developer experience first as you gain a deeper understanding of the business needs of user management. You’ll optimize for customer delight, flexibility, and ease-of-use within a complicated, technical domain.

According to recent reports, collaborate with teammates to design fresh features. You’ll work closely with Product, Design, and Engineering across project lifecycles from ideation to implementation.

Gather requirements. You’ll research the technology and customer impetus behind the features we release. You’ll attain a deep understanding of the problems we solve.

Structure and prototype. You’ll create flows and interactions that make sense of complex information, whether it’s a static component or a multi-page view.

It has been revealed that not settle for less than pixel-perfection. You’ll work with a world-class UI Engineering team to bring your Figma frames to life. You set the bar for quality.

Elevate our design culture. You’ll support and expand the Clerk Design visual language, component library, accessibility practices, design system, and design processes.

You’re a Senior(+) level Product Designer with experience working in authentication, user management, or developer tools. You love your craft. You push Engineers to build experiences they’re unsure if they’re capable of (and you expect them to do the same for you).

You’re in the Americas. The Clerk Design team is spread across the globe; Product Design currently spans UTC+1 to UTC+5:30. You live in a location that is ±3 hours within U.S. Mountain Time (MDT, UTC−06:00).

You have technical fluency. You have a deep understanding of designing interactive software on the web. You don’t need to author production-ready front-end code, but it’s a substantial plus if you can.

Sources indicate that you work iteratively. Your process embodies a “ship and iterate” mentality. You value the quick pace of a growing startup like Clerk.

Recent findings suggest that you own your time. You’re a self-starter who would rather find a tough problem to solve instead of waiting for a fresh task. To be successful at Clerk, you need to make the most of the autonomy you’re given.

In a recent development, 💰 Competitive Salary – We want you to know that we value the skills and experience you bring to the table. We go out of our way to make sure that you feel fairly compensated.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that at the time of the Fresh Planchette article’s circulation in 1886, Charles Kennard was a real estate agent who owned a fertilizer business in Chestertown, Maryland, just across the wide expanse of the Chesapeake Bay from the state’s industrial center of Baltimore. Kennard was born in Delaware on Christmas Eve, 1857, and was eleven years old when he witnessed the “wonderful workings of Planchette” during its ﬁrst great craze. By 1876, he had begun “an investigation of psychical phenomenon” while living in Philadelphia, and his table-rapping experiments continued after he moved to Chestertown that same year.

While Kennard never acknowledged any inﬂuence of the Ohio talking-board reports that appeared in 1886, it was that same year he claimed he envisioned an identical breakthrough, imagining he could receive communications quicker than raps or automatic writing “if words could be spelled by the alphabet.” He struck on what he believed was an original idea: “In 1886 I made a crude board, using a cake board and a table with four legs and a pointer, marking the alphabet and numerals in pencil,” and used the pairing to autonomously spell out messages letter by letter, joining the ranks of Armstrong, Damon, and Long as one of the earliest- known talking-board creators.

Sources indicate that to reﬁne his primitive eﬀorts, Kennard claimed, he visited local cabinetmaker and undertaker Ernest Christian “E. C.” Reiche, a Prussian immigrant whose workshop was adjacent to Kennard’s oﬃce in Chestertown’s Voshell House. He commissioned “about a dozen boards a little neater in appearance than the cake board,” which he then oﬀered for sale locally. He claimed his boards were “always being borrowed by neighbors, and those who purchased the few wanted more,” echoing similar stirrings of interest in Ohio that same year.

By his own account, he petitioned Reiche to continue the productive partnership, but as Kennard later recalled, “I asked him to continue making them for me and we would put the board on the market. This he remarked he would not do. He was too busy to make any more. I would have to get someone else.” Left without a craftsman to manufacture the boards, Kennard’s commercial ambitions sat temporarily idle.

Recent findings suggest that three years later, a competitive marketplace took its toll on Kennard’s fertilizer business, and in February 1890, he relocated his family to Baltimore. There, he opened a newly introduced real estate oﬃce in the Barnum Building and established new headquarters for his fertilizer firm at 220 S. Charles Street. Kennard also rekindled his ambition to commercialize a talking board.10 In an account that echoes Cyrus H. Farley’s attempts to pitch planchettes in Boston, Kennard “highlighted the board to several who could see nothing of the future in it.”.

In a recent development, but a fortuitous meeting came with local attorney and fellow Freemason Elijah Jeﬀerson Bond, who took an intense interest in what he called Kennard’s “witch board.” Bond recounted in later years how he made “important improvements” to Kennard’s design to get it into “marketable shape,” which included a round planchette with a sharply pointed extension that served as an indicator, setting it far apart from the heart-shaped planchettes of yesteryear. He paired the fresh planchette with a board that included two arched rows of the alphabet with a straight line of numbers below, closely matching newspaper illustrations from 1886.

In a recent development, bond added embellishments, including a black dot representing the full moon in one upper corner and a crescent moon in the other, and black stars in the bottom corners. An illustration at the bottom center depicting two men shaking hands—an crucial symbol of fraternity among Freemasons—ﬂanked on each side with the conjunction “Good Bye.”.

The pair partnered with the goal of patenting and manufacturing the idea, with Bond ﬁnancing their earliest eﬀorts with a $500 investment.

Recent findings suggest that the duo’s upcoming talking board had not yet been christened with its iconic name. As the two ironed out the details of the patent design in April 1890, they assembled at Bond’s home with some of his family members. Not satisﬁed with the initial name they had chosen, Charles Kennard proposed they ask the board what it would like to be called, as he later recounted:.

The name Ouija was adopted by Mr. Bond and myself. We called this board by another name until we could secure a better one. One evening about April 1890, while trying the board with a Miss Peters, Mr. Bond’s sister-in-law, in the large boarding house at that time on the corner of Charles and Centre streets, where Mr. Bond boarded, I remarked that we had not yet settled upon a name, and as the board had helped us in other ways, we would ask it to propose one. It spelled out O-U-I-J-A. When I asked the meaning of the word it said “Good Luck.”.

Miss Peters there upon drew upon her neck a chain which had at the end a locket, on it a ﬁgure of a woman and at the top the word “Ouija.” We asked her if she had thought of the name, and she said she had not. We then adopted the word.

In a recent development, ouija was a strange word seemingly without precedent, and its fascinating combination of consonants and vowels, fabricated through Peters’s mediumship, added to the board’s mystique, even as unlikely as it was to have appeared on a locket. Yet her locket is an important clue that her role in Ouija’s naming may have direct ties to the Spiritualist movement.

Industry observers note that peters had no known connection to Spiritualism in her upbringing, but such influence was deeply rooted in her future husband and then suitor Ernest Herbert Donisthorpe Nosworthy. An immigrant from the UK who arrived in January 1888 to work as a traveling salesman, Nosworthy was the seventh child of Frederick Arthur and Eliza Louisa Spry Nosworthy, née Thompson, of Manchester, England, the latter of whom was a talented trance medium who “often attracted large and refined public audiences at Birkenhead by her dramatic powers.”.

Industry observers note that she was the daughter of George Thompson, himself a prominent Spiritualist who sat with Leah Fox in the United States, and had served on the Council of the British National Association of Spiritualists. The younger Nosworthy’s sister, Beatrice, was also regarded as “one of the youngest and one of the best of trance mediums” in England.

The Nosworthy family’s close bonds with one of the most famous mediums of the era may have directly influenced Ouija’s name. The family hosted famous medium Cora Hatch when she visited England, living with them for months at a time on multiple occasions during Nosworthy’s formative school years. Eliza Nosworthy was considered Hatch’s herald and was so close to the family that when Eliza’s prominent father died, the medium adopted him as a new spirit guide with the blessing of the Nosworthy clan.

However, it was another of Hatch’s spirit guides who might have inspired Ouija’s name: the specter of a woman named Ouina, Cora Scott’s most famous contact for her trance mediumship, and Spiritualists considered her a generous spirit who acted as “a messenger of peace and love between the two worlds.” Exposure to Ouina was most certainly in the environment of Ernest Nosworthy’s upbringing, and it may explain the mysterious locket with a woman’s figure and name described by Kennard in his remembrance of Ouija’s naming.

Whatever the case, Bond and Kennard adopted the enigmatic moniker and turned toward securing a patent for their newly named product.

During the mid-1930s, more stories of deaths involving messages received through Ouija made the headlines of American newspapers. The first involved the Turley family of Arizona, when fifteen-year-old Mattie shot her father, Ernes, twice in the back with a shotgun, which resulted in his death a few weeks later.

The news spread far beyond local publications when reports revealed that it was Ouija’s messages that had commanded Mattie to murder her father. The story was further sensationalized by news that her mother and Ernest’s wife, Dorothea, was once voted “the most beautiful girl in America.”.

Widely reprinted articles revealed how Dorothea had become obsessed with a local “handsome cowboy” named Kent Pearce and used the Ouija to manipulate her daughter into murdering her own father so that Dorothea would be free to marry Pearce. All three were charged, although Pearce denied any involvement and was ultimately found not guilty. Mattie pled guilty in juvenile court and was sentenced to an Arizona reform school, while her mother was found guilty and sentenced to prison but was freed three years later.

Another sensational Ouija murder involved the Hurd family of Kansas City in 1935. Family matriarch Nellie received messages through her Ouija that her seventy-seven-year-old husband, Herbert, was “too fond of another woman” and that he had given his secret lover “$15,000 of a hidden fortune.”.

Sources indicate that after receiving the messages, Nellie and her daughter Bertha ambushed Herbert and chained him to his bed before subjecting him to all manner of tortures, including beating him with a revolver, burning the soles of his feet with matches, and stabbing his legs with a dagger. Bertha also set to killing “the children”—three dogs and a cat—with carbon monoxide, which Nellie had commanded.

These horrible acts led to Herbert signing a forced confession admitting to his affair, which the two women signed as “witnesses.” But a few hours later, Nellie momentarily left her gun within Herbert’s reach, and he seized it and shot his wife four times before making his escape.

According to recent reports, police afterward discovered Herbert “running along the street clad only in his pajamas and carrying a still smoking revolver,” and he confessed to police immediately. Nellie died from her wounds, and the courts deter-mined her death to be a “justifiable homicide.” Bertha remained free after Herbert refused to press charges.

As in prior decades, these Ouija-inspired murders sparked a flurry of sensational headlines like “The Ouija Again Spelled Death!” even if Herbert’s actions were an act of self-defense, and helped contribute to the growing chorus of Ouija’s malign and diabolical associations in the media.

Industry observers note that david Brandon Hodge is the author ofSupernatural Machines: The History of Spirit Communication Devices. Hodge is a historian, collector, and author specializing in the history of spirit communication devices. Founder of MysteriousPlanchette.com and curator of the world’s largest archive of séance artifacts, his research has appeared in Smithsonian Magazine and Paranormal Review, and has served as a consultant for museums and exhibitions worldwide, including the acclaimed Supernatural America exhibit at the Minneapolis Institute of Art and the Peabody Essex Museum’s Conjuring the Spirit World exhibit. Hodge has also appeared in many prominent programs as an expert on the occult, including Oddities, Mysteries at the Museum, and Expedition Files, and served as historical consultant and provided séance artifacts for Rick Alverson’s film The Mountain and Lasse Hellström’s biopic Hilma. Hodge is also a respected game designer and lecturer, known for his horror-themed scenarios and his work with Atlas Obscura and Coast to Coast AM. He owns and operates Monkey See, Monkey Do! toy store and Substantial Top Candy Shop in Austin, Texas, where he lives with his two children, Jack and Elliot, and the ghosts of several cats.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 46, of Colorado Springs, Colorado, pleaded guilty in federal court today to 12 hate crimes charges for using Molotov cocktails to attack members of the group Run for Their Lives and others.

As part of the plea agreement, Soliman admitted that on June 1, 2025, he lit and threw two Molotov cocktails into a gathering of the Boulder chapter of Run for Their Lives, a group that organized walks throughout the United States to raise awareness for hostages still held after the October 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel. Soliman further admitted that he targeted the group because of the victims’ actual or perceived Israeli national origin and Jewish religion. The attack killed one person and caused permanent and life-threatening injuries to several others.

According to recent reports, “No one should be subjected to violence because of their religion or national origin,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “With this plea, we hope to deliver a measure of justice to the victims and their families. The Civil Rights Division remains committed to vigorously prosecuting the perpetrators of bias-motivated violence.”.

Sources indicate that “By his own admissions, Mohamed Soliman’s hateful attack on our neighbors in Boulder was antisemitic,” said U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “All Americans should feel free to pursue their faith and way of life without fear that doing so will put their personal safety at risk. Antisemitism erodes the common ties that bind our great nation together and there is no place for it in America. We are grateful for the trust and support of the victims and the Boulder community as we prosecuted this case.”.

“This individual conducted a despicable attack on people he believed to be Jewish or who support Israel, and with today’s plea he is admitting his guilt,” remarked Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI is steadfast in our commitment to protect our communities and uphold the Constitution. We will continue to work with our Justice Department partners to ensure those who harm others or attempt to intimidate those expressing their personal views are held accountable.”.

“The chaos inflicted by this defendant spread its seeds far beyond Pearl Street, Boulder, and Colorado,” noted Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski of the FBI Denver Field Office. “FBI Denver is proud of the role we played in this case alongside our partners in Boulder: We do not tolerate acts of hate and terror against our neighbors. We will continue to work to keep our community safe and seek justice for victims.”.

It has been revealed that for nine of his hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of life in prison, five years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. For the three other hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of 50 years in prison to run consecutive to any other prison term, three years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027.

The FBI Denver Field Office and the Boulder Police Department investigated the case.

Sources indicate that assistant U.S. Attorneys Melissa Basche and Daniel Pastor for the District of Colorado and Trial Attorneys Sarah Howard and Khalil Quinan of the Civil Rights Division’s Criminal Section are prosecuting the case.

The Fourth District Court of Appeal in Florida on Wednesday banned a disbarred Florida attorney convicted of fraud from submitting pro se filings in his case after he allegedly “flooded” a trial court with documents, many generated with artificial intelligence.

After Willie Joe Jones of Florida filed more than 70 documents with a circuit court since April 2025, a panel of judges ordered the clerk of the court to reject any of his future filings unless they are signed by a lawyer in good standing with the Florida Bar.

“Abusive AI filing poses a serious threat to the orderly administration of justice,” the panel wrote.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

James Thomas Ashbacher, 37, of Spring Lake, North Carolina, a former U.S. government contractor, was arrested by the FBI on Tuesday for allegedly leaking national defense information by posting the information on a popular social media site, unlawfully retaining other national defense information at his residence, and stealing night vision goggles from the U.S. Army’s Special Operations Command.

Ashbacher was charged by an indictment unsealed Tuesday with unlawfully transmitting and retaining national defense information and with theft of government property.

According to the indictment, beginning in or about 2021, the defendant worked as an employee of a private organization that provided security and emergency management services at the U.S. Army Special Operations Command facility in Fort Bragg, North Carolina. To perform the required functions of his employment, Ashbacher held a Top Secret security clearance with Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) access.

It has been revealed that as further detailed in the indictment, Ashbacher photographed and removed without authorization videos and photographs containing images of classified military operations and transmitted the materials to a social media site. The classified materials were later re-posted by other people to a second social media site. Ashbacher asked a social media user in a private message to remove some materials and further stated that he was “trying to do some damage control.” A search of Ashbacher’s residence also revealed a classified award write-up that contained additional national defense information, along with a night vision goggle system specific to a military unit within Army Special Operations Command that had been reported missing.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office is investigating the case with substantial assistance from the U.S. Department of the Army’s Criminal Investigative Division.

Trial Attorney Leslie Esbrook of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Logan Liles for the Eastern District of North Carolina are prosecuting the case.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that here are five newly translated works of crime fiction, featuring selfish tourists, corrupt cops, desperate horse racers, antiquities smugglers, and amateur sleuths. Enjoy!

Yves Ravey, Taormina Translated by Alyson Waters (Latest York Review of Books).

Industry observers note that taormina is a ruthless condemnation of our selfish modern era, a road trip novel in which a married couple on vacation in Italy run over a migrant child, then proceed to do….nothing. They do not check on the body. They do not go to the police. They do not accept any form of responsibility. They don’t even bother to cover up their crimes (or at least, they cover for themselves only lazily and ineptly). The only action available to either spouse, by dint of their warped world view, is to blame others for their problems. A vicious gem that wouldn’t feel out of place in mid-century noir, although the story’s catalysts are firmly grounded in the 21st century.

Gustavo Eduardo Abrevaya, The Bullet Inside Me Translated by Andrea G Labinger ( Schaffner Press).

In a recent development, the Bullet Inside Me takes places at the height of Argentina’s Secret War; in this hard-boiled thriller of compromise and conspiracy, the young daughter of a fascist functionary is kidnapped, in a case that threatens the entire dictatorial order. By the same author as the impressive Sanctuary, this one’s just as compelling, and just as vicious.

Genki Kawamura, The Horse and I Translated by Chikako Kobayashi (Flatiron).

A beautiful tale of the lengths we go to for love. In The Horse and Me, a shy clerk forges a deep bond with a racing horse, one coveted by a wealthy rider who seems poised to destroy the stallion’s spirit. Without means of her own, the clerk begins stealing from her own union’s coffers in order to purchase, then maintain, her newfound soulmate. When her colleagues begin to catch on to the thefts, Kawamura’s heroine finds herself backed into a corner and desperate to turn her horse into a champion.

Sacha Naspini, The Witch’s Mouth Translated by Clarissa Botsford  (Europa).

Grave robbing in Tuscany from ancient Etruscan graves has been significant business since before the war, but with new regulations cracking down on antiquities smuggling elsewhere in Italy, the little band of thieves at the center of the novel face new gangs trying to muscle into their territory, renewed inquiries from weary local authorities, and internal divisions that threaten to dissolve their operation entirely.

Indrek Hargla, The Ghost of Rataskaevu Street Translated by Adam Cullen (Pushkin Press).

Recent findings suggest that hargla’s second novel to feature apothecary Melchior, released for the first time in the US this month, takes his hero on a dark journey stretching far into the city’s past. When three different townspeople die just after seeing a ghost, the pharmacist and amateur sleuth decides to dig into the matter. In between brewing tinctures, infusing remedies, and proscribing his usual treatments, Melchior keeps circling back to a house in the center of town, once the setting of a terrible crime, and key to understanding the more recent killings.

According to recent reports, molly Odintz is the managing editor for CrimeReads and the editor of Austin Noir, now available from Akashic Books. She grew up in Austin and worked as a bookseller before becoming a Very Professional Internet Person. She lives in central Texas with her cat, Fritz Lang.

Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland, a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the U.S.
  • Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government and has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months.
  • “Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” mentioned Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland, a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the U.S. Department of State, and the U.S. Department of Justice pleaded guilty today to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia.

Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government and has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months.

“Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” mentioned Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict. Clearance holders pledge undivided loyalty to the United States and bear a legal and moral responsibility to protect classified information. Those who betray this trust will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”.

Recent findings suggest that “For more than two years, Lemma exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security. His guilty plea sends a clear message: those who compromise America’s most sensitive secrets will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable.”.

“Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government,” noted Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States.”.

According to recent reports, “Today’s guilty plea makes clear that any attempt to betray the United States, violate the trust of the American people, and compromise our national security will not be tolerated,” said Assistant Director in Charge Darren B. Cox of the FBI Washington Field Office. “Lemma abused his position of trust and access to some of our nation’s most highly classified information, conspiring with foreign government officials to unlawfully disclose materials protected to the highest level. In doing so, he not only endangered our national security but also betrayed the trust placed in him by the American people.”.

Recent findings suggest that according to court documents, Lemma held a Top Secret U.S. security clearance. From 2021 until his arrest in August 2023, Lemma conspired with senior Ethiopian government officials to collect and transmit dozens of highly classified documents, notes, materials, and photographs, classified up to the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) level, to Ethiopian government officials. Material identified as “Top Secret” means that unauthorized disclosure of the material is reasonably to cause “exceptionally grave damage to the national security” of the United States.

Recent findings suggest that much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia. Lemma’s conspirators included senior officials within political, military, and intelligence branches of the Ethiopian government.

During his espionage activities, Lemma took numerous steps to conceal his conduct. and surreptitiously removed classified documents and information from U.S. government holdings.

Specifically, Lemma wrote notes by hand with classified information and then hand-carried those notes out of secure U.S. government facilities. Additionally, as an IT administrator, Lemma removed electronic versions of classified information from classified U.S. government repositories and then removed the same classified information from secure U.S. government facilities where he worked.

On some occasions, Lemma encouraged his Ethiopian government conspirators to take direct action against paramilitary groups who were fighting the government of Ethiopia. For example, on Dec. 18, 2021, Lemma told one conspirator, “We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia.” Later that day, Lemma shared additional information with his conspirator and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].”.

According to the plea agreement, Lemma agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government. If accepted by the court, Lemma has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months. Sentencing is set for April 14, 2027.

Recent findings suggest that the FBI Washington Field Office investigated the case, with assistance from the U.S. Department of State's Diplomatic Security Service.

According to recent reports, the matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Adam P. Barry for the District of Columbia, and Trial Attorney Kathryn DeMarco of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that fresh research from Stanford University has found that people are increasingly using artificial intelligence to file lawsuits. (Photo by Userba011d64_201/Getty Images).

Fresh research from Stanford University has found that people are increasingly using artificial intelligence to file lawsuits.

It has been revealed that according to the report, which was released by the university’s researchers Thursday, more than a third of civil suits filed in Santa Clara County, California, and San Francisco County this year show signs of AI use. The researchers noted that this doesn’t include debt collection cases.

Sources indicate that among other findings, Stanford’s researchers noted that pro se litigants had higher AI adoption rates. In Santa Clara County, the share of self-represented complaints that showed signs of AI use increased from 19% in 2024 to 72% in 2026. Meanwhile, the share of attorney-filed complaints increased from 5% to 34% during this period.

Industry observers note that researchers also found that the use of AI varies by case type, with employment and business complaints in California showing the highest rates. They noted AI use also varies throughout court filings, with more appearances in the statement of facts and causes of actions sections.

“The sharp rise we document here corroborates that AI in the law is a question of how, not whether,” Stanford’s researchers wrote in the report.

💡 Key Takeaways
