    • According to recent reports, but the justices did not account for one thing, according to Brooklyn Law School Professor Yuvraj Joshi: O’Connor’s later misgivings about that statement.
    • Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

    In June 2023, the court decided Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. University of North Carolina, holding that race-conscious admissions at Harvard and the University of North Carolina violated the Constitution. Chief Justice John Roberts’ majority opinion in the case, along with Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s concurrence, cited Justice Sandra Day O’Connor’s 2003 prediction in Grutter v. Bollinger that “25 years from now, the use of racial preferences will no longer be necessary to further” student body diversity.

    According to recent reports, but the justices did not account for one thing, according to Brooklyn Law School Professor Yuvraj Joshi: O’Connor’s later misgivings about that statement. In interviews with her biographer after she left the court, O’Connor acknowledged that the 25-year figure “may have been a misjudgment.” When asked for a new estimate, she replied, “[t]here’s no timetable. You just don’t know.”.

    Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

    Sources indicate that recommended Citation: Nora Collins, Even justices have regrets, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 20, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/even-justices-have-regrets/.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 24, 2026, 11:32 am CST.

    A Washington superior court judge received an admonishment Friday from the Washington Commission on Judicial Conduct for commenting on “violence from the Native American community,” causing courtroom onlookers to react in shock and offense. (Image from Shutterstock).

    A Washington superior court judge received an admonishment Friday from the Washington Commission on Judicial Conduct for commenting on “violence from the Native American community,” causing courtroom onlookers to react in shock and offense.

    According to recent reports, mason County Superior Court Judge Monty D. Cobb made the remark while sentencing a defendant who pleaded guilty to killing a fellow member of the Skokomish Tribe.

    Cobb said it was “extremely unfortunate that I see way too many acts of violence from the Native community,” according to coverage by Law360.

    Many tribal members were inside the courtroom when Cobb made the statement, and two complaints reported to the Washington Commission on Judicial Conduct prompted a confidential investigation.

    The investigation “determined that the quoted comments caused shock and offense among the onlookers and a sense that respondent was blaming the community for its experience of high rates of violence,” the judicial conduct commission’s report said.

    Cobb admitted to violating two rules: Canon 1, Rules 1.1 and 1.2 of the Washington Code of Judicial Conduct, which requires judges to conduct themselves in a manner that promotes public confidence in the judiciary’s integrity and impartiality and to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

    Sources indicate that the judge’s sanction, in part, includes reading the state’s Code of Judicial Conduct “in its entirety” and confirming in writing. The investigation’s document noted that courtroom observers think that Cobb “does not harbor a bias against Indigenous people or other marginalized groups, and that everyone is treated fairly in his courtroom.”.

    #192960. Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2337 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2337 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • With arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite.
    • Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.
    • Every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    With arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite. Whether you are a Supreme Court follower who usually shunts criminal law to the side, or an experienced criminal law reader who might enjoy some holiday dinner thoughts for your friends and family, this column seeks to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law – and perhaps show why that can be so interesting. To do so, I will scatter some examples from last term, drawn from my recently published Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Cases booklet. When explaining criminal law to your friends or just opining over Thanksgiving dinner, I’d like to show why your mantra should be “crim law is con law” and vice versa.

    Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.

    Every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship. Even non-lawyers know from film and TV that the prosecution’s high burden for proof in a criminal case is beyond a reasonable doubt. But do they know that this is constitutionally required? And perhaps more interesting, that this standard is nowhere, textually, in that document?

    It has been revealed that “[T]he Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime with which he is charged,” wrote Justice William Brennan Jr. for the Winship court. If only all Supreme Court decisions had such clear and succinct rule statements.

    In a recent development, but why is this the rule? It is not found either in the body of the Constitution or in the Bill of Rights, which was adopted soon after the Constitution and focused largely on criminal law protections. Winship‘s answer: because that standard “dates back at least from our early years as a Nation,” “[i]t is now accepted in common law jurisdictions,” it is expressed “in many opinions of this Court,” and it has “long been assumed” to be “constitutionally required.” Thus history, tradition, and precedent support it. Perhaps most fundamentally, a high standard of proof, harder to satisfy than in civil law cases, is essential to fundamental fairness for the public as well as individuals charged with crimes. It is “indispensable to command the respect and confidence of the community” as well as “every individual” exposed to imprisonment. Or, as Justice John Harlan II wrote in an influential concurrence, this standard is “bottomed on a fundamental value determination of our society that it is far worse to convict an innocent man than to let a guilty man go free.”.

    Recent findings suggest that thus, a fundamental premise of criminal law, Winship, is constitutional law too. Moreover, and just by the way, Winship demonstrates that the “incorporation” theory of the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause (that is, applying the Bill of Rights to the states) is not limited to concepts stated expressly in the Bill of Rights itself – as “proof beyond a reasonable doubt” is not. Critics of non-textual constitutional rights – like privacy, a right to travel, a right to refuse medical treatment (like mask wearing?), or even a right to terminate a pregnancy – must confront the application of their literalist theory to proof beyond a reasonable doubt, too. For this reason, I also teach Winship in every constitutional law class.

    There are almost no crimes mentioned in the Constitution.

    This sometimes surprises 1L students (and others). But the goal of the Constitution was to (re)describe a system of government, and form “a more perfect Union” after the prior Articles of Confederation had proved unsatisfactory. It was not to write a criminal code. The states were then (and still are) the primary forum for criminal law.

    So the Constitution defines only one crime, treason (in Article III, section 3). It mentions a few others, like “Bribery” (in Article II, section 4) and “Breach of the Peace” with a general reference to “Felony” (in Article I, section 6). And of course the Impeachment Clause (Article II section 4) mentions “high Crimes and Misdemeanors,” without definition. Again, states were expected to take care of the substantive definition and application of virtually all criminal law. (However, as I explained some years ago, the First Congress in 1790 did enact over two dozen federal crimes.).

    Yet a large focus of the Bill of Rights is criminal procedure.

    Sources indicate that three years after the Constitution was drafted, the Bill of Rights focused on criminal law rights in at least four proposed amendments (the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eighth). I won’t list the multitude of rights captured there, but they form the bulk of all criminal procedure law school classes today. The right to be free from unreasonable governmental searches and compelled self-incrimination, and the rights to counsel, jury trials, and no cruel and unusual punishments – and much more – are all embodied in the Bill of Rights.

    One example from last term: in Villareal v. Texas, the court had to interpret the Sixth Amendment right to “Assistance of Counsel” to decide (unanimously) that a criminal trial judge can order that the defendant not discuss their ongoing testimony with their attorney during an overnight recess.

    According to recent reports, why was the Bill of Rights so focused on criminal procedure rights? It’s a fun question to ask students, or at the Thanksgiving table if things get slow. Sooner or later someone gives the soundbite answer: “because most of the constitution’s framers were crooks.” They were certainly guilty of treason – then and still today a capital (that is, death penalty) offense, as well as other crimes (violence, destruction of property, incitement, and more). Had the revolutionary Framers been captured by the government (the British) they likely would have been hung. Instead, during the course of the revolution, numbers had been tried in absentia, found guilty by officials (not juries), and had their houses searched and occupied by troops. Cruel and unusual torture had been inflicted on some captured compatriots. When constitutional ratifying conventions demanded a bill of rights, protections from unfair criminal processes were therefore topmost on the minds of many drafters (if not perhaps “the People” at the time).

    (Another aside: ask your lawyer friends to compare the content of civil procedure versus criminal procedure classes today. The latter full-semester course is almost entirely constitutional law – I used to call my own crim pro class “Con Law Three.” By contrast, civil procedure classes, also a full semester, focus largely on the nitty-gritty details of federal rules, only occasionally wandering into statutes or the Constitution.).

    Industry observers note that in addition to the four explicitly criminal-focused amendments, you might then add general constitutional ideas that are bound to capture some criminal law cases: the First, Second, Third, and Ninth Amendments. The First Amendment’s direction, that “Congress shall make no law” regarding (“respecting”) or abridging freedoms of religion, speech, and the press, is a constitutional law command against criminal laws as well as civil. So too is a protection of a right to keep and bear arms, and to not have government troops quartered in “any” house (not just your own).

    And then consider the “great generalities” of the Constitution.

    In his 1921 Storrs Lectures at Yale Law School (subsequently published as “The Nature of the Judicial Process”), future Supreme Court Justice (and then New York Court of Appeals Judge) Benjamin Cardozo discussed “the great generalities of the Constitution.” Among these, the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the 14th Amendment are huge sources of criminal law doctrine. Just last term, for example, the procedural steps required to apply the Equal Protection Clause against racial (and other) bias in jury selection, and the idea that due process and judicial integrity requires a “miscarriage of justice” exception to guilty plea waivers, received focused Supreme Court attention (in Pitchford v. Cain and Hunter v. United States, respectively).

    Criminal law cases focused on the meaning and application of these broad constitutional requirements arise regularly almost every Supreme Court term. Indeed, as I advise my students every year (again I aspire to teach with a smile, not didactic cynicism): no matter what arguments you make on the defense side of a criminal case, always add the words “and in violation of due process” to preserve at least a thread of a constitutional argument that you may not even perceive at the moment.

    According to recent reports, in addition to equal protection and due process, I (and others) would add the Ninth Amendment, which speaks of unspecified “rights … retained by the people.” Justices have sometimes suggested that the Ninth and Tenth Amendments state nothing but “truism[s],” while other Supreme Court decisions have relied (at least in part) on the Ninth. For some, invocation of the Ninth Amendment may provoke if not laughter (it having been referred to by one academic as a “constitutional jester”), then a distinctly conservative or “originalist” rejection. Yet other conservative scholars such as John Yoo and Calvin Massey (my late former colleague) have written expansively about it. As Randy Barnett has argued, the Ninth Amendment “means what it indicates,” and is “a significant guarantee of individual liberty.” If that is so, then it is (or could be) another source of criminal law protection for criminal defendants.

    For example, Griswold v. Connecticut recognized a constitutional right to privacy in the criminal law context, resting in part (and almost entirely for three justices) on the Ninth Amendment. Less controversially, perhaps, Chief Justice Warren Burger later invoked the amendment in the 1980 case of Richmond Newspapers v. Virginia to support an “unarticulated” constitutional right for the public (and the press) to attend criminal trials. And in 2000, even Justice Antonin Scalia agreed (in a solo dissent to Troxel v. Granville, a non-criminal case) that the Ninth Amendment recognizes unenumerated rights. When you tell your Thanksgiving dinner companions that criminal law is constitutional law, don’t forget the Ninth Amendment.

    So criminal law is, very often, constitutional law.

    Industry observers note that thus it should be unsurprising (as detailed in my Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Law booklet) that 22 of the court’s merits decisions last term that address criminal law involved elements of constitutional law (17 fully argued cases plus five summary (unargued) decisions). That’s a substantial percentage of the court’s entire merits opinions docket, roughly a quarter or more.

    Statutory criminal law cases also often involve constitutional law.

    According to recent reports, by now I hope that you are persuaded: criminal law is (often) constitutional law. “But wait – there’s more!” When you combine the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause with the oft-cited judicial doctrine of constitutional avoidance, criminal cases requiring statutory interpretation also fall into this category. That is, these are criminal law cases that involve consideration of constitutional law. Advocates in statutory cases often raise potential constitutional objections to a criminal statute or to its application in their case, or they may raise constitutional law ideas in favor of their preferred interpretation. In addition, an understanding of constitutional doctrine can be necessary to properly evaluate the merits of a statutory claim. The bottom line is that, in many statutory criminal cases, explication or consideration of constitutional law is necessary or helpful to explain the result.

    Just a few examples from last term: In Barrett v. United States, the court had to mine the details of double jeopardy doctrine to agree, unanimously, that a statute could be interpreted as not permitting two convictions for a single act, thereby avoiding a constitutional problem. In Olivier v. City of Brandon, the court had to examine Olivier’s constitutional claims in order to decide whether the federal civil rights statutes were a proper vehicle for him to sue under. And in Whitton v. Dixon, the court had to briefly explain the constitutional Giglio doctrine, regarding a prosecutor’s failure to disclose exculpatory impeachment information, to reverse an application of the federal habeas corpus statue.

    Sources indicate that immigration cases also often require constitutional law, either to dispose of the merits or to resolve statutory concerns in them. Last term’s birthright citizenship case, Trump v. Barbara, is the most obvious example. Because immigration and criminal law cases are often intertwined – consider recent ICE arrests, detentions, and criminal violation grounds for removal – I include them in my annual review as well as the purview of this column. And even civil cases that I consider related to criminal law often require consideration of constitutional law concepts. For example, last term’s Hencely v. Fluor Corp., rejecting a claim of government contractor immunity, required consideration of constitutional preemption doctrine.

    In other words, criminal law mixed with constitutional law is everywhere.

    It has been revealed that last week, many of us were focused on the details of elections around the country, big and small. And next week, after Thanksgiving, will be chock full of criminal law and related Supreme Court oral arguments. So I’ve tried to give you a break today, and provide a few thoughts that are, perhaps, entertaining, or provocative, or at least interesting ways to navigate your mealtime gatherings (rather than focusing on the usual subjects). For some of you, perhaps this column has simply demonstrated what you already considered obvious; or perhaps it has opened interesting linkages in your mind between constitutional law and criminal law. In any case, thanks for reading this far. Next week I hope you are fortunate enough to breathe relaxing breaths, give thanks, and dwell not on legal minutiae but on what really matters.

    Rory Little has been teaching Constitutional and Criminal Law topics at UC Law SF (formerly Hastings) for over 30 years, after 12 years of practice.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Clutch is at a pivotal moment. We're growing significantly year over year, and we need more connective tissue to keep pace. We're hiring a Senior Manager, Business Operations to connect the commercial side of the house, so the teams that win, onboard, and retain our customers work from the same facts and toward the same goals. This role sits in Finance.

    In a recent development, this is a people manager role. You'll lead our Revenue Operations (RevOps) team and act as an operating partner to senior leaders across Sales, Marketing, Customer Success, Implementation, People, and Finance. Together with the RevOps team, you own the shared language of the business (definitions, data, and processes) so commercial teams make decisions from one view of it.

    When something notable doesn't have an owner yet, it lands with you: a partnership strategy, a new commercial model, or pricing and margin guidance for leadership. This is a fast-moving startup. We're building toward a much larger company but we aren't one yet, and most of this role has no playbook. You'll define the process, build the tool, and hand it to the team. If you want established structure, this likely isn't the role.

    Sources indicate that you'll report to the Director of Business Operations and work directly with senior leaders across the company as a neutral partner to every function rather than an advocate for one. Your work will be visible, and it will significantly influence how we make commercial decisions.

    It has been revealed that you'll lead a small, high-ownership RevOps team that runs the systems and data our commercial teams depend on, and creates leverage for them to do their jobs even better. The team doesn't just own systems. They build automation, tooling, and processes, and they're close partners to Sales and Marketing. You'll coach them, set priorities, and open up more strategic scope, while giving them real autonomy.

    Learn the business end to end: the revenue funnel, the customer lifecycle, how each commercial team works day to day, and where decisions get stuck.

    Build trust with your RevOps team: learn the work they own, and set priorities and team rhythms together.

    Deliver the first version of client-level margin and cost-to-serve, the analysis that grounds our pricing strategy.

    Develop a first point of view on pricing and packaging for revenue leadership, built on that analysis.

    Put AI to work in your own workflow from week one, and identify the first set of manual, repetitive processes across the commercial teams worth automating.

    Stand up a first version of a deal desk, including an approval workflow, pricing and discount guardrails, and standard commercial terms.

    Partner with Sales and Marketing leaders as they prepare for the monthly business review: pressure-test their aims and point out risks, then solve them with the RevOps team by creating new processes, tooling, or automation.

    Build on the strength of the RevOps team: prioritize its roadmap against business outcomes and take on more strategic work together.

    Launch your first AI-enabled workflows or automations that remove manual reporting or reconciliation for the commercial teams, with time saved tracked.

    Have a team whose output and standards hold, with the processes, tooling, and automation you've built running without you in the room.

    Have AI-enabled, self-serve tooling that commercial teams use day to day, with measurable time savings.

    Be the person leadership trusts to pick up the next vital thing that doesn't have an owner yet.

    5-8 years of total experience that combines consulting or banking with time as an operator inside a firm.

    Experience managing people: you've coached ICs, given direct feedback, made tough talent calls, and built team rhythms.

    Industry observers note that startup experience. You've worked in a fast-moving, ever-changing environment where structure wasn't already there, and you built it. This is not a role for someone whose experience is only at large, established enterprises.

    Industry observers note that strong analytical and financial modeling skills, including forecasting. You're very comfortable building models in spreadsheets from scratch, and they hold up to scrutiny. You use AI to move faster and sharpen your work, and you have the foundational modeling knowledge to know when its output is wrong.

    Data-first and self-sufficient. You open the dataset before you build the slide, you're always looking for more data to test an idea, and you're comfortable getting into raw data yourself. You use AI to analyze it faster and know enough to check its work.

    Commercial acumen: you can read commercial terms, spot the problematic ones, and reason about pricing, discounting, margin, and deal structure.

    A clear communicator who can walk an executive through a messy problem and leave them with a decision, and who is just as effective working alongside an AE, a CSM, or an engineer.

    Industry observers note that comfort with ambiguity. When something isn't set up yet, your instinct is to build it, not to wait for it. You create structure, manage competing priorities, and pivot when things change.

    Relentless follow-through: you close loops, and people stop checking on what you've said you'll do.

    A partner's temperament: you challenge constructively without taking sides, you surface problems early, and you resolve cross-team conflict without escalating it.

    Industry experience in fintech, financial services, lending, banking, or credit unions.

    Please note that this role may evolve as our business needs change, so we appreciate your flexibility and adaptability.

    Remote Flexibility: Enjoy the freedom of remote work from anywhere, balancing life and career seamlessly.

    Unforgettable Off-Sites: Twice a year, bond with colleagues in exciting destinations, fostering teamwork and fresh ideas.

    Paid Time Off: Enjoy flexible PTO days yearly for relaxation and rejuvenation.

    Stock Options: Joining us means having a stake in our success, so you'll receive stock options as part of your compensation package.

    Home Office Setup: Create your ideal workspace with a dedicated budget for home office essentials.

    Work Trip Budget: Grow personally and professionally with a budget for work-related trips and co-working.

    Health Coverage: Prioritize your well-being with comprehensive health and dental insurance plans.

    Clutch is a revolutionary vertical SaaS firm, proudly backed by Andreessen Horowitz (A16z), aimed at revolutionizing the way Credit Unions engage and change the lives of their members. As a champion of financial well-being, we address the urgent need for affordable lending solutions in an era where the average American grapples with over $155,000 in household debt. Unlike traditional financial institutions, Clutch develops software to turn Credit Unions into FinTech lenders and leverage their balance sheets to responsibly lend to over 130M Americans. Our mission extends beyond mere financial transactions; we strive to fundamentally enhance the way credit unions interact with their members. By integrating cutting-edge technologies and user-centric designs, we help credit unions provide seamless digital experiences that are on par with leading tech companies. This approach not only preserves but revitalizes the longstanding tradition of community and member-focused service inherent to credit unions.

    Clutch is an equal opportunity employer. All applicants will be considered for employment without attention to race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, veteran or disability status.

    Law firm apologizes to truckers for ‘serial killer’ ad

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A Texas law firm is apologizing for an ad in Maxim magazine that created such an outcry among truckers that truck stops pulled the publication from their shelves.
    • According to recent reports, the full-page ad for San Antonio law firm Villarreal & Begum revealed a picture of a truck cab beneath the words “serial killer.” Both the law firm and Maxim are apologizing for the ad after Pilot Flying J and TravelCenters of America pulled the magazine from their shelves.
    • The copy read: “3,561 people died on America’s highways last year.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A Texas law firm is apologizing for an ad in Maxim magazine that created such an outcry among truckers that truck stops pulled the publication from their shelves.

    According to recent reports, the full-page ad for San Antonio law firm Villarreal & Begum revealed a picture of a truck cab beneath the words “serial killer.” Both the law firm and Maxim are apologizing for the ad after Pilot Flying J and TravelCenters of America pulled the magazine from their shelves. Publications with stories include HDT Trucking Info, TheTrucker.com, CSPNet.com, KIROTV.com and LandLinemag.com.

    The copy read: “3,561 people died on America’s highways last year. Another 2.36 million were injured. You need a law firm you can Trust. You need Experience. You need Strength. You need Villarreal & Begum. We’re proven leaders in prosecuting cases involving death and catastrophic injury.”.

    In its statement, the law firm states it never intended “to disparage the hardworking Americans that drive tractor-trailers for a living. Our intent was to reach out to those individuals who have been involved in catastrophic accidents as a result of irresponsible drivers. The ad was inartfully created, and we could see how it may have caused our message to be misconstrued. We recognize the service that truck drivers provide to this nation and acknowledge that most truck drivers are safe and responsible drivers.”.

    Maxim also issued a statement saying the ad “does not reflect the beliefs or opinions of the people at this magazine, which recently has begun operating under latest ownership.” The ad has been pulled from Maxim’s digital copy and replaced with facts about the trucking industry.

    California owed water consumers hearings before 2021 drought cutbacks

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • An appellate panel mentioned the water companies weren't given a meaningful hearing before the state ordered them to cut back on diversions in 2021.
    • (CN) â The Ninth Circuit on Tuesday reinstated due process claims from a group of Northern California water rights holders who were ordered to curtail their river water diversions in 2021 during a drought emergency.
    • In a unanimous opinion, the three-judge panel reversed a trial judge’s dismissal of the due process claims by Stanford Vina Ranch Irrigation, Los Molinos Mutual Water and Peyton Pacific, which between them hold the bulk of the water rights along Deer Creek and Mill Creek, two tributaries of the Sacramento River.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    An appellate panel mentioned the water companies weren't given a meaningful hearing before the state ordered them to cut back on diversions in 2021.

    (CN) â The Ninth Circuit on Tuesday reinstated due process claims from a group of Northern California water rights holders who were ordered to curtail their river water diversions in 2021 during a drought emergency.

    In a unanimous opinion, the three-judge panel reversed a trial judge’s dismissal of the due process claims by Stanford Vina Ranch Irrigation, Los Molinos Mutual Water and Peyton Pacific, which between them hold the bulk of the water rights along Deer Creek and Mill Creek, two tributaries of the Sacramento River.

    Whereas the trial judge in Sacramento had agreed with the State Water Resources Control Board that its emergency regulations and curtailment orders were “legislative,” the appellate panel concluded they were “adjudicatory,” meaning the water companies are entitled to a meaningful hearing before being deprived of their right to divert water from the two creeks.

    According to recent reports, “Whether an action is legislative or adjudicatory turns on the character of the action, rather than its label,” U.S. Circuit Judge Lawrence VanDyke wrote. “Actions affecting large areas with undifferentiated populations are considered legislative.”.

    “By contrast, adjudicatory actions target or exceptionally affect a few persons on an individual basis,” the Donald Trump appointee added.

    While legislative regulations and orders don’t require individualized hearings, due process requires that adjudicative decisions provide notice and predeprivation hearings.

    “The reason for requiring hearings for adjudicatory but not legislative decisionmaking is fundamentally a practical one: As the Supreme Court explained, hearings become impracticable when the affected group is too large to give a direct voice in the adoption of a challenged regulation,” VanDyke noted.

    In this case, 22 water rights holders along the Deer Creek and Mill Creek were affected by the 2021 emergency order to cut back their diversions, but the plaintiffs claim they were given only a five-minute public comment period, with no opportunity to cross-examine the state’s witnesses supporting the regulations.

    This, VanDyke said, was not a meaningful hearing.

    U.S. Circuit Judge John Owens, a Barack Obama appointee, and U.S. Circuit Judge Danielle Forrest, a Trump appointee, joined in the decision.

    In a separate memorandum disposition, the panel upheld the trial judge’s dismissal of the plaintiffs’ takings claims under the Fifth Amendment because they could have sought compensation for their losses through an inverse condemnation lawsuit in California state court.

    In a recent development, the appeal focused on water rights held in Mill Creek and Deer Creek in Tehama County. Those rights allow the companies to divert water for some 11,000 acres of land with orchards, pasture and other uses.

    In April 2021, after a lack of winter storms left the state’s water reservoirs depleted, California Governor Gavin Newsom declared a drought state of emergency, leading state agencies to take action and protect salmon, steelhead and other fish.

    Jackson Minasian, an attorney for the plaintiffs, argued at a hearing before the Ninth Circuit panel in August that California had stopped the diversions four times in seven years. The state will have future droughts and curtailment orders for the water, and when that happens, the attorney noted, the companies should get a due process hearing and compensation for the taking of the water.

    âThe salmon and steelhead come back every year,â Minasian remarked. âTheyâre taking it for free and they keep doing it.â.

    Minasian and representatives of the California Attorney General’s Office didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

    #192948. Latest Update: The Supreme Court and profanity

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2225 w)

    Latest Update: The Supreme Court and profanity

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2225 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, around 2 p.m.
    • In a recent development, the station later said it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl.
    • Before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, around 2 p.m. on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio. New York’s WBAI, a nonprofit radio station, was airing a program on modern attitudes toward language. Near the end, the station played George Carlin’s “Filthy Words” routine, which begins with the comedian saying he’d been thinking about “the words you couldn’t say on the public airwaves; the ones you definitely wouldn’t say, ever.” He went on to repeat those words several times, contrasting them with words like “bastards,” “hell,” and “damn,” which were mostly acceptable, and showing how even some of his list of seven were perfectly fine in other contexts. His point was to show the absurdity of profanity.

    In a recent development, the station later said it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl. Carlin, the station explained, was doing more than “mouthing obscenities.” He was “using words to satirize as harmless and essentially silly our attitudes towards those words.”.

    Before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense. But about a month later, John Douglas complained to the Federal Communications Commission about the transmission which he said was “garbage” and had been broadcast in the presence of his “young son.” He was the only listener to do so. A member of Morality in Media who frequently listened to the station to “see how far” they’d go, Douglas later acknowledged that he had laughed out loud at the bit but “did not appreciate WBIA’s ‘smart-alecky’ on-air provocations.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the previous year, Carlin had been arrested after performing an earlier version of the same routine, but a judge threw out the charge. This time, the FCC found the broadcast “indecent,” and put its order in the station’s license file.

    That order ended up before the Supreme Court.

    Industry observers note that early in its order, the FCC acknowledged that Congress had forbade it from censoring broadcasts. But Congress had also prohibited the broadcast of “obscene, indecent, or profane” language, and the Commission thought Carlin’s broadcast fit the bill. In the FCC’s view, the ban on “indecent” language covered not just obscenity, but also patently offensive language when there was a reasonable risk of children listening. Late at night, when children were unlikely to be listening, the same material might be okay if it appeared in a work of serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.

    Two commissioners thought even that was too permissive. Charlotte Reid believed “this language to be totally inappropriate for broadcast at anytime” and thought the commission’s standard did “not go far enough.” Commissioner James Quello took much the same view. “Garbage is garbage,” he wrote, whether children were listening or not.

    In a recent development, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, however, set aside the order in a 2-1 vote, with one judge believing it violated the statutory ban on censorship and the other saying it violated the First Amendment. The FCC appealed to the Supreme Court.

    At oral argument, which was held in April of 1978, several justices made their distaste for Carlin’s bit plain. When Pacifica’s lawyer stressed that the station had warned listeners beforehand and aired the monologue as part of an educational program about language, Chief Justice Warren Burger incredulously asked, “This is educational in your view?” And when counsel defended the material’s artistic value, Justice Thurgood Marshall responded, “Well, I’m not an expert, but if that’s artistic, deliver me.” Justice William Rehnquist, for his part, tested the limits of Pacifica’s position with a hypothetical involving a single four-letter word repeated for an hour. Would the FCC be powerless to prohibit that? Justice John Paul Stevens, however, seemed troubled by the potential reach of the FCC’s position, given that the prohibition on indecency could be enforced through criminal law.

    According to recent reports, one striking exchange concerned the Justice Department’s position to argue separately, and more narrowly, than the FCC. The solicitor general’s office urged that the First Amendment prevented the government from barring particular words outright for a substantial part of the day without regard to context, even if the FCC could constitutionally regulate “indecency” to some extent. Rehnquist sharply asked why the Justice Department was arguing against the FCC, what interest it had in seeking a narrow construction of an act of Congress, and whether the solicitor general, as the government’s lawyer, could ever argue that an act of Congress was unconstitutional.

    Sources indicate that justice Lewis Powell also pressed the DOJ on the reasons behind its departure from the FCC, noting that the DOJ had supported the FCC in the court below. “That is true, and that is an embarrassment to us,” Deputy Solicitor General Louis Claiborne acknowledged, suggesting it was because the matter had been handled there by the Antitrust Division rather than the Criminal Division. Another explanation, which he did not mention, was that the administration had changed.

    Industry observers note that the court ultimately ruled 5-4 that the FCC could constitutionally treat this broadcast as “indecent” under the governing statute, and that the government could constitutionally prohibit indecency even though it fell short of legal obscenity. Stevens wrote for Burger, Justice Harry Blackmun, Powell, and Rehnquist, having apparently struggled with the case and flip-flopped before settling against Pacifica. The Commission had treated the piece as a nuisance, and, as the court had observed in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., a nuisance could be as simple as “a pig in the parlor instead of the barnyard.” He concluded that “when the Commission finds that a pig has entered the parlor, the exercise of its regulatory power does not depend on proof that the pig is obscene.” Though the holding expanded the government’s power to regulate speech, Stevens emphasized broadcasting’s pervasive presence in the home and its accessibility to children, the fact the piece was broadcast during the daytime, and the narrowness of the holding. He did not address late night broadcasts or the “occasional expletive.”.

    Stevens had only three votes for some parts of his opinion. Powell, joined by Blackmun, wrote separately to object to Stevens’ suggestion that the level of protection that speech receives should depend on a judge’s perception of that speech’s value. For them, the combination of repeated, patently offensive language, an afternoon broadcast, and children’s ready access was enough to resolve the case. Powell also addressed the concern that the decision could end up “reduc[ing] the adult population . . . to [hearing] only what is fit for children”: adults could buy tapes or hear the same words at theaters.

    Sources indicate that justice Potter Stewart dissented, joined by Justices William Brennan, Byron White, and Marshall. Stewart would have resolved the case on statutory grounds. He read “indecent” to reach only obscene material, and everyone agreed that Carlin’s monologue fell outside that category. His opinion recalled his concurrence in Jacobellis v. Ohio, where he voted to overturn an obscenity conviction for showing a French film with an explicit love scene. Stewart understood obscenity narrowly, but declined to define it, famously observing in that case, “I know it when I see it, and the motion picture involved in this case is not that.”.

    Recent findings suggest that brennan wrote a separate dissent, joined by Marshall, that went further. He agreed with Stewart on the statute and said he would ordinarily refrain from addressing the constitutional question, but he found “the Court’s misapplication of fundamental First Amendment principles so patent, and its attempt to impose its notions of propriety on the whole of the American people so misguided,” that he was “unable to remain silent.”.

    Brennan disputed the analogy between a radio broadcast and an intrusion into the home. Listeners voluntarily turn on the radio, and they can voluntarily turn it off. In perhaps his sharpest passage, he wrote:.

    According to recent reports, brennan also questioned the majority’s reliance on protecting children. He read the court’s precedents as allowing the government to shield children from material that was obscene as to them. In his view, Carlin’s routine fell outside that category. Keeping it off the radio during the afternoon cut off access for adults as well as children. And while the majority had invoked parents’ right to raise their children as they saw fit, Brennan thought the FCC had somewhat ironically made the choice for them.

    Finally, he remained unconvinced that the court’s reasoning would reach only cases like Carlin’s. Among the things it could sweep in were “literary works, novels, poems, and plays by the likes of Shakespeare, Joyce, Hemingway, Ben Jonson, Henry Fielding, Robert Burns, and Chaucer,” “a good deal of political speech, such as the Nixon tapes,” and even portions of the Bible. In his view, the public, and not the court, should have the power to weed out “worthless and offensive” speech in a marketplace “unsullied by the censor’s hand.”.

    In a recent development, brennan and Marshall had joined together in another Supreme Court opinion involving the F-word. In Cohen v. California, they joined Justice John Harlan II’s opinion protecting the right to wear a jacket emblazoned with “Fuck the Draft.” Stewart joined it too (not surprisingly, Burger and Blackmun dissented). Brennan brought Cohen straight into his Pacifica dissent; as he made clear, changing the words can change what the speaker communicates, something that applies especially well to Carlin because the taboo words were themselves the subject of the routine. And Brennan thought telling listeners to buy a record or pay to see Carlin live missed what it meant to hear the routine on the radio.

    In a recent development, in closing, Brennan wrote that the majority had only “confirm[ed] Carlin’s prescience as a social commentator.” (It was interesting that Marshall, who sounded distinctly unimpressed by the claim of artistic merit at oral argument, joined him, perhaps especially here.) As Brennan pointed out, Carlin had made fun of the rules about which words you could say on the air, and the court had exemplified the very attitude he was satirizing. To top it all off: Appended to the opinion is the transcript of Carlin’s routine, giving his “indecent” words a permanent home in the U.S. Reports.

    Industry observers note that at the 2002 Billboard Music Awards on Fox, Cher dispatched the critics who’d spent decades predicting her downfall with “So f*** ’em.” At the 2003 awards, Nicole Richie asked whether anyone had tried getting cow manure out of a Prada purse, then used the F-word to describe how hard it was. The next year, after Bono called U2’s Golden Globe win “really, really f***ing brilliant,” the FCC confirmed that even a single expletive could be indecent, and it later applied that approach to the two earlier Fox broadcasts.

    In a recent development, in 2009, the Supreme Court took up the dispute in FCC v. Fox Television Stations. Writing for a 5-4 majority, Justice Antonin Scalia held that the FCC had adequately explained its change in policy under the Administrative Procedure Act, leaving the First Amendment question open. Justice Clarence Thomas joined the majority but wrote separately to question Pacifica’s holding. On remand, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit struck down the policy as unconstitutionally vague.

    According to recent reports, the case returned to the Supreme Court in 2012 and all eight participating justices agreed on the result (Justice Sonia Sotomayor recused herself). Justice Anthony Kennedy’s opinion held that the FCC had failed to give Fox fair notice that fleeting expletives could trigger an indecency finding, but once again left both Pacifica and the First Amendment question open. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote separately to say that Pacifica was wrong from the start and deserved reconsideration. But while the court has had several cases involving curse words since, it has yet to take up the question directly.

    In 2004, the FCC dismissed complaints related to the airing of Saving Private Ryan on the basis that the film’s curse words helped convey the soldiers’ experience. But just two years later, it slapped a station with $15,000 in fines for airing a Martin Scorsese documentary about Blues music that contained profanity. In 2020, the FCC received over 1,300 complaints about Jennifer Lopez and Shakira’s halftime show, though it never took any action against the network. And in February 2026, FCC requested transcripts of Bad Bunny’s Superbowl halftime performance before ultimately finding no violation.

    Half a century after Carlin’s seven dirty words, the FCC’s continued and seemingly arbitrary application of its indecency laws demonstrates the prescience of Brennan’s dissent and the need to finally answer the question of whether the Constitution prohibits the “dominant culture” from trying to force “groups who do not share its mores to conform to its way of acting, thinking, and speaking.”.

    Anastasia Boden is a Senior Attorney at the Pacific Legal Foundation, where she brings civil rights lawsuits that advance the Constitution’s promises of equality and economic opportunity.

    A federal judge rejected two nursesâ efforts to dismiss claims that their handling of Ben Cunninghamâs medical care at San Diego Central Jail contributed to his death weeks after he fell from a top bunk in a cell.

    SAN DIEGO (CN) âÂ A fall from a top bunk in a San Diego jail left a man suffering from alcoholism with potential injuries that may have caused his death a few weeks later.

    The nurses responsible for his care are still on the hook for a lawsuit filed by his family against San Diego County, a federal judge ruled.

    The family members of Ben Cunningham say the man was in the hospital for serious liver and kidney challenges, but left â against medical advice â hours before police officers arrested him and took him to the San Diego Central Jail on Jan. 28, 2024. They say Cunningham should have been transported back to the hospital or placed in a medical observation bed at the jail.

    In a recent development, the family members say Cunningham was instead given a top bunk in a three-bunk bed in a jail cell, despite his disclosure of his serious medical needs and obvious inebriation. Cunningham fell from the top bunk a few hours later, lost consciousness and was unable to stand on his own, they say. But he was not taken to an emergency room until more than 24 hours later.

    According to recent reports, family members say the nurse who was in charge of his intake, Chasity Beene, and the nurse responsible for monitoring his condition after he fell, Brenda Bebal, contributed to his death. The family claims deliberate indifference to medical needs, negligence and wrongful death, among others.

    Sources indicate that beene argues the familyâs complaint does not establish her personal involvement in Cunninghamâs intake and falls short of federal pleading standards. She also states the plaintiffsâ claims donât describe an intentional decision on her part.

    U.S. District Judge Cathy Bencivengo disagreed.

    âThe allegations that Beene knew that decedent was detoxing and had existing medical concerns, knew San Diego Central Jailâs relevant policies and procedures, and that a reasonable nurse practitioner would have known of the dangers in a similar situation, yet did not send decedent to the hospital, place him in a medical observation bed or flag him for a low bunk are sufficient to plausibly allege an intentional decision by Beene regarding decedentâs medical care,â Bencivengo, a Barack Obama appointee, wrote on Monday.

    Industry observers note that âGiven the alleged policy and procedure, it is plausible that a reasonable nurse practitioner performing decedentâs medical evaluation âwould have appreciated the high degree of risk involvedâ and, at a minimum, flagged him for a low bunk,â she continued. âBeeneâs decision not to order any of these three treatment options does not transform her actions into something unintentional.â.

    In a recent development, cunninghamâs family says Bebal ordered only that his vitals be checked every other day after his fall. As a result, there was an unreasonably long delay in taking him to the hospital, which caused his death, they say.

    Bebal argues the symptoms of serious harm did not develop until after her evaluation, so she was unaware of them.

    In a recent development, âThis argument mischaracterizes plaintiffsâ allegations,â the judge wrote. âPlaintiffs do not allege that these later symptoms are what signaled the substantial risk of serious harm, but that the immediate effects of the fall â decedent hitting his head, his loss of consciousness and his inability to stand â put Bebal on notice of a substantial risk of serious harm. Plaintiffs also claim that Bebal did not conduct a real evaluation of decedent and that given the fall and decedentâs medical history, Bebalâs decision not to conduct a more thorough evaluation is what also put decedent at a substantial risk of serious harm.â.

    Sources indicate that the nurses both argue the claims against them were untimely because they were filed more than a year after Cunningham died, but Bencivengo disagreed with this too. They filed their lawsuit within a year of his death certificate being issued, she ruled.

    The plaintiffs originally believed Cunningham had been beaten by cellmates or corrections officers.

    The family members also named the San Diego County Sheriffâs Office, its deputies and medical officers in their lawsuit.

    Recent findings suggest that “We, including Ben’s loved ones, are heartened and validated by the court’s ruling,” noted Lauren Mellano, an attorney for McKenzie Scott Civil Rights & Criminal Defense Lawyers, in an email. “In proceeding forward on all claims, we hope that Ben’s case will be a lesson to the county and for-profit contractors such as Naphcare and Correctional Healthcare Partners that medical providers and deputies must begin to work as a team and treat the safety of people in the county jails as their top priority.”.

    Spokespersons for the defendants did not respond to requests for comment.

    In September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion. In her acceptance speech, Jackson discussed Brennan’s role as the Supreme Court became more conservative, noting that he “believed that even his dissents could make a difference and remind the nation that the pursuit of equal justice under law is an ongoing effort.” Jackson indicated that she agreed with that idea, telling the audience that she saw “dissent[s] as more than just a disagreement with the outcome of a case, I see them as an expression of faith in the future and a demonstration of hope.” As she put it, “However desolate the moment feels, we who write for a future age have hope that the noble and collective work of bending the long arc of the law toward justice will continue.”.

    Since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view. Although she has been consistently part of the court’s liberal bloc, even among the three Democratic appointees she has forged a unique role. As her invocation of Brennan suggests, it often appears that her goal is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision and to speak to the public directly – even if she does so without the support of her fellow liberals.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    LOS ANGELES (CN) âÂ A Los Angeles Superior Court judge noted Tuesday she was inclined remove LA County and a local water district from a mass tort involving thousands of plaintiffs suing over the 2025 Palisades Fire, which claimed 12 lives and destroyed more than 6,000 buildings.

    Recent findings suggest that in a tentative ruling that was not made public, Superior Court Judge Samantha Jessner indicated she would likely sustain a demurrer filed by the county and water agency. The plaintiffs have argued those two public entities had recently upgraded a water system to better withstand a large wildfire.

    Following a 1993 fire in Malibu, the water district, which is managed by the county, installed emergency backup generators capable of pushing water uphill in the case of a power outage. However, the district decided to not bury the newly introduced power lines underground or otherwise protect them. As a result, the plaintiffs say, the lines melted during the 2025 blaze, rendering the recent improvements all but worthless.

    Sources indicate that “They elected to choose a system that was not resistant to fire occurring,” plaintiffs’ attorney Peter McNulty told the judge at a hearing Tuesday. “If you get money and design a system, you canât cheap out and not protect that system.”.

    He later added: “To not do that, that is a failure they caused to occur. Itâs not just that a couple of conduits melted. Itâs that the whole system didnât deliver the protection it was supposed to.”.

    It has been revealed that last week, a federal jury convicted 30-year-old Jonathan Rinderknecht, a former Uber drier, of two counts of arson for setting the Lachman Fire shortly after midnight on Fresh Yearâs Day, 2025. That relatively small brush fire was easily suppressed, but remained smoldering and reignited into the much larger Palisades Fire thanks to especially dry conditions and strong winds.

    Much of the plaintiffs’ master complaint focuses on the state of California and the city of Los Angeles and what they claim is their failure to monitor the area of the Lachman Fire, and for not adequately managing the vegetation in the area. They also fault the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power for leaving the 117-million-gallon Santa Ynez Reservoir empty.

    Sources indicate that their claims also include inverse condemnation against the county and the water district, for the unprotected power lines. Mira Hashmall, the attorney representing the county, argued inverse condemnation can only apply to public improvements that damage private property âÂ and not public improvements that don’t do a good enough job of protecting the public.

    Industry observers note that “It’s not intended for loosey-goosey concepts of negligence,” Hasmall stated. Should the plaintiffs’ theory become the standard, she said, “public entities would become insurers” and “disincentive creative backup plans that may not work.”.

    Jessner did not say when she would issue a final ruling.

    After the hearing, McNulty said the claim against the county was a small but significant part of the case, “but weâll live to fight another day if the judge sticks with her tentative.”.

    Breaking: 2 Montgomery County magnet stories raise 1 question about access

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • “Minorities in Magnets” was the winner of the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice’s 2026 High School Civil Rights Film Competition.
    • Recent findings suggest that A high school filmmaker saw a problem in Montgomery County, Maryland’s selective programs: Lack of representation of students of color had an impact on their educational experiences.
    • Although these stories involve different programs and raise different questions, they share an notable issue: How do we determine whether an admissions system provides fair access to educational opportunities, and what evidence should matter?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    “Minorities in Magnets” was the winner of the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice’s 2026 High School Civil Rights Film Competition.

    Recent findings suggest that A high school filmmaker saw a problem in Montgomery County, Maryland’s selective programs: Lack of representation of students of color had an impact on their educational experiences. At nearly the same time, a lawsuit challenging admissions to the county’s middle school magnet programs reached the U.S. Supreme Court.

    Although these stories involve different programs and raise different questions, they share an notable issue: How do we determine whether an admissions system provides fair access to educational opportunities, and what evidence should matter?

    In a recent development, the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice recognized Minorities in Magnets, directed by Toftaa Fedhaa, as the first place winner of the section’s 2026 High School Civil Rights Film Competition. Her film explores the experiences of students of color in the Montgomery County Public Schools’ high school magnet programs and the effects of their underrepresentation.

    Separately, on Oct. 19, the Supreme Court agreed to hear Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education. The case concerns admissions to four selective middle school magnet programs, not the high school programs discussed in the film.

    While the court did not rule on whether the district’s admissions policy is discriminatory, it agreed to consider a narrower legal question about the evidence plaintiffs must present when challenging a facially neutral admissions policy as racially discriminatory.

    The Association for Education Fairness alleges that Montgomery County’s admissions policies intentionally disadvantaged Asian American students. The school district maintains that its admissions system is designed to provide equitable access to rigorous educational opportunities.

    In a recent development, after initially challenging a “field test,” the plaintiffs challenged a revised lottery-based system introduced for the 2021-2022 school year. That system screened students for their potential to benefit from enriched instruction and then used a lottery to assign students to magnet programs or enriched instruction at their neighborhood schools.

    The federal district court dismissed the challenge to the revised plan, finding that the plaintiffs had not adequately alleged discriminatory effect or intent. The 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Richmond, Virginia, affirmed, applying circuit precedent on disparate impact allegations.

    The Supreme Court will now consider whether a plaintiff challenging a facially neutral admissions policy must demonstrate that the affected group experienced an aggregate “disparate impact” compared with its share of the applicant pool.

    Put simply, “disparate impact” refers to a policy that produces unequal outcomes for a particular group, even when the policy does not expressly classify individuals by race. An equal protection challenge also raises the question of discriminatory purpose.

    The court’s decision will address the legal standards governing these types of claims and whether a particular showing of aggregate impact is required before such a claim may proceed, not whether Montgomery County’s policy ultimately violates the Constitution. The court has not yet decided the merits of the case.

    The film underscores why the conversation should not only focus exclusively on admissions policies, statistics and legal standards but should also consider the voices and experiences of students.

    The file and the lawsuit should not be confused or treated as evidence of one another. They involve different grade levels, programs and legal questions. The experiences described in the film do not establish what happened in the middle school admissions process, just as the allegations in the lawsuit do not resolve the concerns raised by high school students.

    Although selective educational programs can open doors to advanced coursework, specialized instruction and opportunities that shape a student’s academic future, simply making a program available to everyone does not necessarily mean everyone has an equal opportunity to participate.

    We must also consider who knows these programs exist, how students are identified and encouraged to apply, what barriers may discourage participation, and whether students feel represented and welcome once they are admitted.

    According to recent reports, these are important questions for educators, families, policymakers and communities to consider. They may also inform legal analysis, although the applicable legal standards determine what evidence is relevant to a particular claim.

    For lawyers, the Supreme Court case highlights the importance of understanding how statistical evidence, applicant pools and allegations of discriminatory intent intersect when challenging facially neutral policies. It also reinforces the need to examine the specific admissions process and how that process may have changed over time. The court’s decision may affect how courts evaluate statistical evidence in challenges to facially neutral admissions policies.

    For school officials, families and advocates, the broader questions are equally notable:.

    • How are students identified and informed about selective educational opportunities?

    • What criteria determine eligibility and admission?

    • Are admissions outcomes regularly examined across schools and student populations?

    • Are the policies and measures used to assess access transparent and understandable?

    These questions deserve attention regardless of how the Supreme Court ultimately resolves the legal glitch before it.

    The case is also a reminder that we must distinguish between allegations in a lawsuit, a school district’s stated reasons for its policies, procedural court decisions, and a final ruling on the merits. Understanding those distinctions is essential to an informed discussion.

    The winning film, Minorities in Magnets, brings student perspectives into a debate that is often reduced to admissions criteria and demographic statistics. The Supreme Court will address a specific legal question about the evidence required in an equal protection challenge.

    Recent findings suggest that neither alone answers the broader question of what meaningful educational opportunity should look like. But they invite a broader conversation about how communities define opportunity, how they measure access, and how they respond when students say the system is not working for them.

    As lawyers and members of our communities, we have an obligation to listen, ask difficult questions, and examine whether the systems we create are providing genuine opportunities for all students.

    Ultimately, educational access is about more than who gets admitted. It is also about who gets the opportunity to succeed, who feels that they belong, and whether every student has a fair chance to reach their full potential.

    It has been revealed that mario A. Sulllivan is the immediate past chair of the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice and a name partner at Johnson & Sullivan in Chicago.

    This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

    #192934. The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1831 w)
