    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1831 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • On November 10, The New York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v.
    • According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    On November 10, The New York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v. Heller, in which the court held that there was an individual right to possess firearms. The essence of the piece is that Scalia used the phrase “dangerous and unusual” to describe those weapons not protected by the right to keep and bear arms, attributing this terminology primarily (or perhaps solely) to the 18th century British jurist William Blackstone. Yet Blackstone’s writings instead use the phrase “dangerous or unusual.”.

    According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.

    Recent findings suggest that the Times story has reverberated quickly, with strong backlash from conservative lawyers and scholars. Such disagreements have focused largely on the specific citation Scalia used. Law professor Jonathan Adler, for example, has argued that the citation to Blackstone was one among many, and additional sources that Scalia cited used the “and” formulation. Others have responded that Scalia was anything but sloppy, which would be especially true when it came to such an influential and crucial source.

    It has been revealed that both sides, though, seem to be burying the lede. In my view, this is a story not about historical errors or the nuances of legal citation. Rather, it is about how judicial dicta that was never intended to lay down broad, permanent rules has taken on a life of its own, and how other justices on the Supreme Court subsequently canonized Scalia’s stray language by turning it into a “test” that would govern any number of future cases – when it’s not at all clear Scalia ever contemplated this or would have endorsed any such thing.

    It has been revealed that as most law students and lawyers are well aware, the holding-dicta distinction is deeply rooted in American jurisprudence: generally speaking, the holding is the analysis necessary to resolve the actual case before the court, and everything else in an opinion is dicta (this comes from the Latin phrase “obiter dictum,” or “said in passing”). Fundamental to that distinction is that dicta, while it may be persuasive, is not precedential. As Chief Justice John Marshall wrote in 1821, the reason for not deferring blindly to dicta is “obvious”:.

    The late Judge Richard Posner once similarly emphasized the risk that dicta “can be misleading if carelessly lifted from the case-specific contexts in which they were originally uttered … That is why courts in assessing the binding effect of previous decisions distinguish between the dicta, which are the inessential parts of the opinion, and the holding.” Circuits vary in their approach to Supreme Court dicta, generally deferring more heavily to such language when they find it thoroughly considered or supported, but the court is, of course, never bound by its own dicta.

    Industry observers note that in fact, Scalia himself was no fan of relying heavily on dicta from prior Supreme Court decisions. In a 1993 opinion, he criticized a group of dissenting justices by noting that their position found “support, if at all, only in the dicta of this Court’s opinions.” This was, in Scalia’s view, as good as no support at all. Indeed, Scalia rejected reliance on “drive-by … rulings” not fully considered by the issuing court, even if not purely dicta. In his 2015 decision for the court in Kerry v. Din, Scalia excoriated a proposition advanced in a dissenting opinion as resting solely on “dictum in a footnote” and then observed that “[t]he footnoted dictum that Justice Breyer proposes to elevate to constitutional law is a dangerous doctrine.” He further joined opinions that rejected prior dicta as unprincipled, especially when greater investigation revealed reasons for caution.

    According to recent reports, scalia’s position was nuanced – for example, he once joined a dissent by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg that endorsed reliance on certain dictum as persuasive – yet a cautious approach to dicta is consistent with his broader judicial philosophy as well. He was at times willing to jettison even precedential decisions squarely applicable to the case at hand when those decisions were contrary to original public meaning. Unconsidered dicta, presumably, would then be far lower in the pecking order.

    Recent findings suggest that returning to Heller and the phrase at issue, it’s hard to argue that the “dangerous and unusual” passage from Heller is anything but dicta. The issue in Heller was whether a Washington, D.C. ordinance “generally prohibit[ing] the possession of handguns” violated the Second Amendment, or if there was an individual right to keep arms for one’s self-defense. Scalia’s majority opinion answered in the affirmative, as “the American people have considered the handgun to be the quintessential self-defense weapon.” D.C. never argued that handguns were entirely exempt from protection because they were especially dangerous. The question of dangerous and/or unusual weapons was not at issue in the case; accordingly, it wasn’t thoroughly investigated through the adversarial process.

    Rather, after canvassing the historical evidence and concluding it supported an individual-rights view of the Second Amendment, Scalia turned to the nature of the right he had just explicated. In three short paragraphs not necessary to the holding, he explained why the amendment did not authorize gun keeping-and-carrying by anyone in any circumstance; rather history revealed limitations on the right, such as “the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’”.

    Whatever the purpose of this section – Justice John Paul Stevens later suggested the language was proposed by Justice Anthony Kennedy (the crucial fifth vote in Heller) in exchange for joining the majority – it was far from necessary to resolve the case at hand.

    So how did such dicta become relevant? In the 2016 case Caetano v. Massachusetts, decided after Scalia had passed away, the justices unanimously overturned a Massachusetts Supreme Court decision upholding that state’s ban on stun guns in a criminal prosecution of a woman who used this weapon to defend herself from an abusive ex-boyfriend. Justice Samuel Alito issued a concurring opinion (joined by Justice Clarence Thomas) that performed an interesting maneuver. Seizing on the fact that the per curiam opinion in that case referenced Scalia’s “dangerous and unusual” formulation, Alito turned Scalia’s language into a doctrinal test: “As the per curiam opinion recognizes, this is a conjunctive test: A weapon may not be banned unless it is both dangerous and unusual.” But the per curiam had done no such thing; rather, that opinion simply cited the passage in Heller as referring to one limitation on the right to keep and bear arms. And the per curiam stated that the lower court in that case had faltered by concluding that any weapon not in common use in 1791 was per se unusual, not by failing to use a conjunctive test.

    (Ironically, Alito has his own well-publicized objections to giving past Supreme Court dicta undue veneration – his opinion for the court in Dobbs heavily suggested that Roe’s viability framework was entitled to less weight in the stare decisis analysis because it was initially mere dicta, “the Court’s own brainchild [for which n]either party advocated.”).

    In a recent development, from there, the “dangerous and unusual” language took on a life of its own. In 2022’s Newly introduced York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, in which the court struck down New York’s concealed-carry law, the majority set forth a test for Second Amendment constitutionality privileging historical evidence above all else. At the first step of that test, a court determines whether the conduct at problem is protected by the right to keep and bear arms, which is where the exclusion of dangerous and/or unusual weapons becomes relevant. If the banned weapon is not protected by the Second Amendment (for, say, being “dangerous and unusual”), a constitutional challenge is dead on arrival. If, on the other hand, the plaintiff can show the weapons are protected, then the burden switches to the government to provide historical evidence to support its regulation. (The consequences may be even greater, as some have argued that “usualness” (or “common use”) conclusively establishes not only threshold protection for the weapon but also that any legislative ban is ahistorical and thus unconstitutional.).

    This test has divided the judiciary in recent years. For example, a Massachusetts federal judge evaluating a challenge to that state’s AR-15 ban recognized the apparent disconnect between Heller and Blackstone but nevertheless noted that “the Supreme Court has expressly stated . . .that the relevant tradition is one of regulating ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’” The Massachusetts judge found these weapons were not in “common use,” and, in any event, a historical tradition of responding to technological advances by regulating specific weapons supported the ban. By contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit interpreted Scalia’s language to signal that widespread ownership of AR-15s and large-capacity magazines meant any legislative attempt to ban them was unconstitutional. The “dangerous and unusual” framework has led other judges on a search for ownership statistics and sales data to assess a weapon’s popularity, triggering sharp debate over whether a test that ultimately turns on commonality is even workable.

    According to recent reports, this is particularly relevant since the court is at the moment preparing to hear oral argument in Viramontes v. Cook County, a Second Amendment challenge to state and local bans on AR-15s, on December 2. While the recent attention to Scalia’s citation may trigger discussion at oral argument, most justices are now likely to treat “dangerous and unusual” as an established standard and ownership statistics as definitive proof that AR-15s are not unusual and thus protected. Absent from this, however, will be the fact that this standard did not emerge from any well-reasoned, litigation-tested analysis making it deserve deference in the first place – especially under Scalia’s own approach to judging.

    The debate over Scalia’s Blackstone citation, then, has obscured a more key problem: the Supreme Court’s decision to treat its past dicta as doctrine that can settle the outcome of cases on which the court has never passed.

    Andrew Willinger is an Assistant Professor at Georgia State University College of Law, where he teaches constitutional law and civil procedure.

    Recommended Citation: Andrew Willinger, The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 23, 2026, 10:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-second-amendment-and-an-unusually-dangerous-approach-to-dicta/.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A judge found the governor's office failed to prove executive privilege covers the records, rejecting its broad "candid private advice" pitch to keep them secret.
    • (CN) â Iowa Governor Kim Reynoldsâ office must turn over four withheld staff communication emails to the stateâs largest newspaper, an Iowa county judge ruled in an order released Tuesday.
    • The Des Moines Register has long sought records surrounding Reynoldsâ appearance before a House panel, where she testified on states’ efforts paralleling those of the White Houseâs Department of Government Efficiency.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A judge found the governor's office failed to prove executive privilege covers the records, rejecting its broad "candid private advice" pitch to keep them secret.

    (CN) â Iowa Governor Kim Reynoldsâ office must turn over four withheld staff communication emails to the stateâs largest newspaper, an Iowa county judge ruled in an order released Tuesday.

    The Des Moines Register has long sought records surrounding Reynoldsâ appearance before a House panel, where she testified on states’ efforts paralleling those of the White Houseâs Department of Government Efficiency.

    The paper prevailed on the bottom line in the order â which was issued Monday â as Polk County District Judge Jason Walke ruled Reynoldsâ office failed to prove executive privilege shields the underlying documents.

    The judge notably held the Iowa Office of the Governor does enjoy some level of executive privilege in specific circumstances under state law, just not in this case.

    In order to obtain such privilege against producing open records, Walke held the office must show âclear and convincing evidenceâ that disclosure would not be in the public interest and would âsubstantially and irreparablyâ limit the executive branchâs ability to function.

    Upon reviewing all four withheld documents covering topics like government efficiency, immigration, gender identity, diversity, equity and inclusion and education funding, Walke found the office did not meet this heavy burden as those matters have been of public interest for years.

    The judge ordered the office to produce the requested documents within 30 days.

    Reynoldsâ office asked the judge in an August summary judgment hearing to declare the emails protected by the same privilege awarded to Iowa General Assembly members â arguing that âcandid adviceâ between the governor and her advisers should be shielded.

    In a snarky rebuttal, Walke noted candid is just another way to say âexpressing opinions, feelings or thoughts.â.

    âThose statements of the executive privilege are, to be blunt, so vague and varied as to be of really no assistance,â Walke remarked in the ruling, noting that interpretation of executive privilege would apply to an email advising the governor to consider serving âhealthy oatmealâ at state functions instead of âunhealthy pop tarts.â.

    âThat would, after all, be âcandid advice to the governor,’â he added.

    During the relevant February 2025 hearing, U.S. Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, an Illinois Democrat, asked Reynolds whether she agreed with claims by former Trump adviser Michael Flynn and then-DOGE head Elon Musk that Lutheran Family Services and its affiliates were a âmoney-laundering operation.â.

    After the hearing, the Register filed an open-records request with Reynoldsâ office seeking staff emails mentioning âLutheranâ and âmoney laundering,â as well as any communications with Lutheran Services of Iowa CEO Renee Hardman.

    Reynoldsâ office turned over hundreds of documents, but refused to hand over four specific emails identified by the office as âmedia-prepâ messages â later suing the newspaper in April 2025 to prevent the release of the emails, prompting a swift counterclaim.

    Walke resolved the matter as a whole in his order and cancelled a scheduled December trial, though the possibility of an appeal looms even as Reynolds is set to leave office in under two months time.

    Though Reynoldsâ office lost its bid to withhold the records, Walkeâs order settled that executive privilege exists under state statute, and laid out how courts evaluate it using existing open records law.

    âThis ruling would be the same if the party seeking the docs was not one of the most respected newspapers in the country,â Walke wrote.

    He added that records the governor did not personally read or write are not automatically excluded from executive privilege.

    The Register previously argued executive privilege does not exist in Iowa â noting legislative privilege involves communications between lawmakers and constituents, not between government staffers.

    Walke rejected the paperâs request for attorney fees, damages or other penalties, finding the governorâs office acted in good faith in seeking an injunction over an unsettled legal question.

    Reynolds’ office did not respond to an initial request for comment, and the Register referred to its article published Tuesday in lieu of comment.

    Experts warn public urgency will fade quickly if health care officials don't practice more consistent, year round engagement with patients and the broader public.

    (CN) â Public opinion is swinging back in favor of childhood vaccines as measles, once eradicated from the U.S., makes a comeback across the continent.

    Truncating a downward slope since 2001, 72% of respondents to a Gallup poll released Tuesday called childhood vaccinations âvery importantâ or âextremely important,â compared to 69% in 2024. The share of those who answered âextremely importantâ rose by seven percentage points.

    Gallup released the data, collected in early October, just one week after world health officials unveiled that the U.S. has lost its measles-free status. The highly contagious virus once relegated to medical textbooks has spread â largely among the unvaccinated â at the highest rate in more than 30 years.

    There have been 43 fresh outbreaks and at least 5,838 confirmed cases of measles across the country in 2026, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. As the virus ravages communities, only 17% of respondents remarked they believed vaccines to be more dangerous than the diseases they prevent â statistically similar to 2024âs results but a far cry from the mere 6% who believed so in 2001.

    The reversal comes after more than a year of outbreaks and efforts by the Trump administration to revoke federal childhood vaccine recommendations, which resulted in multiple lawsuits still working through the courts.

    Jyoti Pathak, dean of Arizona State Universityâs School of Technology for Public Health, said public trust naturally ebbs and flows with the current level of exposure.

    Recent findings suggest that âVaccines are often victims of their own success,â Pathak stated in an interview. âWhen measles stayed largely out of sight for decades, many parents naturally focused on potential side effects rather than an illness they rarely encountered. As U.S. measles cases reach a 35-year high and local exposure notices hit communities across the country, the real-world risks of hospitalization and severe complications become tangible again.â.

    Pathak warned that while recent outbreaks may wake people up, public urgency fades just as rapidly as it enters the headlines, like it did during the smaller spike in 2019.

    Sustaining confidence after the immediate threat subsides requires moving away from reactive, crisis-only warnings toward consistent, year-round engagement led by trusted âlocal messengers like pediatricians, school nurses and community health workers,â Pathak noted.

    According to recent reports, still, attitudes about childhood vaccinations remain less favorable than in earlier decades. In 2001, 94% of people remarked vaccinations were very or extremely important. And a large gap still remains between Republicans and Democrats.

    Just 50% of Republicans believe that vaccines are very important, compared to 91% of Democrats. The data also shows that Republicans are more likely to say theyâve heard only about the negative effects of vaccines and have not heard about the benefits.

    Pathak declined to look at the problem through a purely partisan lens, instead blaming a broader shift against institutional trust fueled in part by fragmented information ecosystems.

    âOver the past decade â and accelerating sharply during the Covid-19 pandemic â public health guidance became entangled in wider debates over mandates, while algorithmic social media feeds sorted Americans into very different information environments,â Pathak mentioned.

    To close the gap in vaccine confidence, Pathak says public health experts must âlisten to familiesâ specific questions without judgment, communicate openly about both protective benefits and rare side effects, and use modern data/technology tools to spot emerging confusion early.â.

    âTop-down directives and dense statistical tables rarely persuade worried parents,â he added.

    In November 2025, Kennedy Jr. directed the CDC to revise its website to suggest a connection between vaccines and autism, a departure from previous guidance. President Donald Trump also linked the childhood vaccine schedule and autism while signing an executive order that revised vaccine recommendations in August 2026.

    While those who do not believe vaccines cause autism rose from 36% to 46% since 2024, 16% of respondents say they believe vaccines do cause autism â the highest percentage since 2015.

    âSocial media stories still travel much faster than epidemiological studies â especially when parents navigating an autism diagnosis are searching online for answers,â Pathak said. âData alone is not enough unless clinicians and public health communicators share it with empathy, clarity and respect.â.

    Just in the U.S., the CDC estimates routine childhood vaccinations have prevented approximately 508 million cases of illness, 32 million hospitalizations and over 1.1 million deaths, generating $2.7 trillion in societal savings.

    Associate Clinical Professor Nicole Ferschke at Northern Arizona University said vaccination is one of the best ways to prevent the further spread of measles.

    âIt protects the person who is vaccinated as well as contributes to herd immunity, which protects individuals who cannot be vaccinated for specific medical reasons,â she told Courthouse News.

    Ferschke echoed Pathakâs concerns that the short-term uptick will not be sustained without increased efforts to improve trust in healthcare nationwide, which includes increasing access to vaccines and transparent, evidence-based communication.

    #192928. Breaking: What do these Supreme Court plaintiffs have in common?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3136 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: What do these Supreme Court plaintiffs have in common?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3136 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that last term in Little v.
    • On Tuesdays for the past few months, we have dedicated the “Closer Look” section of SCOTUSblog’s daily newsletter to covering the story of some of the most famous plaintiffs behind landmark Supreme Court cases.
    • Now 16 installments in, we thought it would be a good time to take a step back and assess what’s been learned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that last term in Little v. Hecox, which concerned whether states could bar transgender female athletes from participating in girl’s and women’s sports, Justice Sonia Sotomayor asked Idaho Solicitor General Alan Hurst: “Do you dispute that having a case named after you makes your infamy ... live forever? ... You don't think that Brown and any of the other named plaintiffs that we have in famous cases dr[ew] … attention to those people as people?” Sotomayor asked the question in the context of Hecox requesting that the Supreme Court dismiss the case, citing, in part, “negative public scrutiny ... because of this litigation.”.

    On Tuesdays for the past few months, we have dedicated the “Closer Look” section of SCOTUSblog’s daily newsletter to covering the story of some of the most famous plaintiffs behind landmark Supreme Court cases.

    Now 16 installments in, we thought it would be a good time to take a step back and assess what’s been learned. In this article, we offer a glimpse at the lives of a baker, a farmer, an executive director at Planned Parenthood, two students, and a leader of the Ku Klux Klan. But besides having interesting (and sometimes disturbing) life stories, what do they all have in common? Each asked the Supreme Court to answer one of the most fundamental questions of all: Where does government power end and personal liberty begin?

    Joseph Lochner: Lochner v. New York.

    Let’s start with Joseph Lochner. Lochner immigrated from Bavaria, Germany, to the United States at the age of 20 in 1882, and settled in Utica, Upcoming York. He sought employment in the bakery industry; around 1890, he opened his own small, family bakeshop in Utica.

    It has been revealed that during this time, efforts emerged across New York to regulate the conditions of bakery workers after an article written by Edward Marshall, a muckraker, revealed their unsanitary conditions. In 1895, the state passed The Bakeshop Act, which aimed to prevent biscuit, cake, and bread bakers from working more than 10 hours a day or 60 hours a week.

    Twice charged with violating this statute, Lochner decided to challenge the law on the grounds that it violated the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause, which he argued protected the economic liberty to enter into such a contract with one’s employees.

    Sources indicate that lochner ultimately made its way to the Supreme Court and presented the court with the question of whether Latest York’s law violated Lochner’s fundamental liberty interest. Everyone agreed that, under the powers reserved to the states, New York certainly had some powers to regulate general welfare. The question was whether New York had gone too far in restricting an employer’s freedom to contract with his employees.

    Industry observers note that for some, the Latest York statute was perfectly legitimate and a function of the democratic process. As then-future Judge Learned Hand argued, “we should not have the inconsistent spectacle of a government, in theory representative, which distrusted the courage and justice of its representatives, and put its faith in a [judiciary] which was, and ought to be, the least representative of popular feeling." Put simply, if there was a legitimate legislative purpose for the law, then according to Hand, courts should defer to what the elected representatives decided.

    In what was seen even at the time as a surprising decision, the Supreme Court sided with Lochner five to four. “The general right to make a contract in relation to his business is part of the liberty of the individual protected by the Fourteenth Amendment of the Federal Constitution,” wrote Justice Rufus Peckham in his majority opinion.

    While Peckham conceded there could be grounds for the legislature to implement regulations to improve workplace safety, he also held there was not sufficient evidence that the Bakeshop Act’s hour-limits would actually improve worker health. And if the statute was upheld, Peckham argued that it would open up almost every aspect of life to state regulation.

    In dissent, Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes lampooned the majority, writing that “a constitution is not intended to embody a particular economic theory.”.

    Lochner has since been abandoned and its reasoning rejected by most legal scholars. Yet defenders remain. Law Professor Randy Barnett, for example, argues for a theory that if the government wants to institute a regulation of liberty, “the burden of proof is more or less on the legislature.” This gets at a fundamental debate in constitutional law: Why do certain civil liberties not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution get heightened scrutiny while economic liberty does not?

    In a recent development, as for Lochner himself, he returned to private life and continued to run his bakery. He died on December 14, 1939.

    According to recent reports, roscoe Filburn: Wickard v. Filburn.

    Recent findings suggest that few cases are more detested by constitutional conservatives than Wickard v. Filburn. Roscoe Curtiss Filburn was born on August 2, 1902, in Dayton, Ohio. A fifth-generation farmer, Filburn grew crops and raised livestock. The crops included winter wheat, which was, in part, for personal use.

    It has been revealed that in a New Deal effort to help prop up the struggling agriculture industry, Congress enacted the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938. The secretary of Agriculture would create a national allotment of acres that could be used to produce wheat. The allotment would then be appropriated to states and ultimately to individual farmers. Filburn’s allotment in 1940 was for 11.1 acres of wheat, but he planted 23 acres of it. Administrators of the AAA fined Filburn 49 cents per excess bushel that he grew and placed a lien of $117.11 on his entire wheat yield.

    Filburn challenged the excess penalty in court on the grounds that the statute was passed under the Commerce Clause, which states that Congress shall have the power to “regulate Commerce ... among the several States.” Filburn contended that his activities did not implicate interstate commerce.

    If the winter wheat was grown by Filburn and never crossed state lines, could Congress then regulate it?

    In a recent development, the Supreme Court sided against Filburn, holding unanimously that his economic activities, taken in the aggregate, would have a substantial effect on interstate commerce. The logic went as follows: If Filburn grew his own wheat, then he would not need to purchase wheat on the open market; and if many farmers did this, it would undermine Congress’ efforts to stabilize the price of crops. “That [Filburn’s] own contribution to the demand for wheat may be trivial by itself is not enough to remove him from the scope of federal regulation where, as here, his contribution, taken together with that of many others similarly situated, is far from trivial,” explained Justice Robert Jackson.

    According to recent reports, the decision remains controversial to this day (to put it mildly). Critics of Filburn argue that the decision gives Congress near unlimited power to enact regulations under the Commerce Clause, effectively allowing Congress to regulate every aspect of people’s lives and largely mooting the powers reserved to the states. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the Supreme Court appeared ready to reduce the Commerce Clause’s reach, striking down two statutes as exceeding Congress’ power. But it has not invalidated a law on these grounds since. (Although the Supreme Court in National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius held that Congress lacked the power to enact the Affordable Care Act’s individual mandate under the Commerce Clause, it ultimately upheld the mandate under Congress’ power to tax.).

    According to recent reports, filburn returned to private life after his Supreme Court case and rarely spoke about it. During the 1950s, he purchased Beverly Shop, a woman’s beauty store, and, in 1966, Filburn convinced the other successors to his grandparent’s 640-acre farm to collectively sell the land to developers. He died on October 4, 1987, at the age of 85.

    In a recent development, estelle Griswold: Griswold v. Connecticut.

    Estelle Griswold was born on June 8, 1900, in Hartford, Connecticut. A talented singer, she attended The Hartt School of Music, a music conservatory in Hartford. In 1935, she moved to Washington, D.C. for her husband’s job, where she volunteered at a doctor’s office and worked at George Washington University as a lab instructor.

    Sources indicate that in the 1950s, Griswold moved to Latest Haven and a few years later was offered the role of executive director of the Planned Parenthood League of Connecticut. In 1961, she opened a birth control clinic in New Haven, along with a doctor, but was convicted and fined $100 in violation of the Barnum Act, a Connecticut law that prohibited the use of “any drug, medicine, article, or instrument” to prevent conception (and, yes, named after that Barnum).

    It has been revealed that griswold challenged her conviction on the grounds that the Barnum Act was unconstitutional. As some of the act’s legal defenders pointed out, although many may regard such a law as a profound violation of personal autonomy, the Constitution lacks any mention of “privacy,” never mind preventative contraception. Put succinctly by Justice Potter Stewart in his dissenting opinion, “I can find no such general right of privacy in the Bill of Rights, in any other part of the Constitution, or in any case ever before decided by this Court.” (To be fair, the idea of the Constitution containing a right to privacy was not latest when Griswold was decided; albeit in a different context, Justice Louis Brandeis had articulated such a right in an 1890 law review article.).

    Recent findings suggest that in a 7-2 decision, the Supreme Court found the Barnum Act unconstitutional and held that married couples have a right to contraception as part of an implicit right to privacy. Justice William Douglas contended that the lack of its enumeration does not preclude that right from existing under the Constitution, akin to precedent in which the court found a parental right to send their children to religious schools. According to Douglas, “specific guarantees in the Bill of Rights have penumbras, formed by emanations from those guarantees that help give them life and substance. ... Various guarantees create zones of privacy.”.

    It has been revealed that while Douglas’ vote for a constitutional right to privacy won the day, his articulation of penumbras and emanations did not fare so well (although Justice Clarence Thomas apparently still pays “tribute” to this language with a sign in his office reading “Please do not emanate into the penumbra”). Rather, concurring in the judgement, Justice John Harlan II argued that the “teachings of history [and] solid recognition of the basic values that underlie our society” based in the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause supported the decision in Griswold, a standard that has since become the prevailing defense of the right to privacy and served as a foundation for later Supreme Court decisions such as Roe v. Wade and Obergefell v. Hodges.

    According to recent reports, soon after the decision was revealed, the PPLC clinic reopened, but Griswold stepped down as executive director as she had fallen out of favor with some members of the organization due to its continued financial struggles. Griswold passed away on August 13, 1981, in Fort Myers, Florida at age 81 and was posthumously inducted into the Connecticut Women’s Hall of Fame in 1994.

    The Tinkers: Tinker v. Des Moines.

    Another major area of constitutional controversy has involved the limits of free speech in the classroom context. Although such cases continue to crop up (BONG HiTS 4 JESUS, anyone?), the modern foundation for them was laid in 1969’s Tinker v. Des Moines. Which brings us to the Tinkers.

    John Tinker was born in 1950, and his sister, Mary Beth, was born in 1952. They grew up in Atlantic, Iowa, where their father was the pastor of a Methodist church. In November 1965, John, then a high schooler, attended a rally in opposition to the Vietnam War in Washington, D.C. On the way back to Iowa, John and other protesters agreed to wear black armbands to protest the war and to mourn the deaths on both sides.

    More than 50 students across public schools in Des Moines planned to wear black armbands to school on December 16, 1965, in support of Sen. Robert Kennedy’s proposed Christmas truce. However, local principals instituted a policy that all students wearing black armbands would be asked to remove them.

    It has been revealed that on December 16, 1965, Mary Beth wore a black armband to Warren Harding Junior High School and was suspended after she refused to take it off. The next day, John wore a black armband to North High School and was also suspended after declining to remove it.

    In March 1966, the Tinkers sued, arguing the schools violated their constitutional rights. Specifically, the Tinkers contended that the public schools were an arm of the state and they were therefore bound by the First Amendment.

    Allan Herrick, arguing for Des Moines at the Supreme Court, contended that the school district must be in a position to “preserve order and to avoid this disturbance and disruption in the school room.” As Justice Thomas would argue decades later in Morse v. Frederick, “through the legal doctrine of in loco parentis [in the place of a parent], courts [historically] upheld the right of schools to discipline students, to enforce rules, and to maintain order.”.

    It has been revealed that in February 1969, the Supreme Court sided with the Tinkers, holding that students do not “shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate.” In its decision, written by Justice Abe Fortas, the court established the substantial disruption test, which sets the necessary conditions for regulating student speech. To do so, the school must be able to reasonably foretell “material and substantial interference” with other students’ learning or the school’s operations. Fortas held that the school district failed to show that the Tinkers’ protests resulted in any material disruption.

    Sources indicate that to this day, Tinker receives mixed reviews. Supporters of an expansive interpretation of the First Amendment tend to support the principles in Tinker and argue that they should be even more broadly applied; critics, such as Justice Thomas, are skeptical that students have First Amendment rights at all. (As Justice Hugo Black put it in his Tinker dissent, “It may be that the Nation has outworn the old-fashioned slogan that ‘children are to be seen, not heard,’ but one may, I hope, be permitted to harbor the thought that taxpayers send children to school on the premise that, at their age, they need to learn, not teach.”).

    After the Supreme Court’s decision, John Tinker remained active in anti-Vietnam war demonstrations and later became the manager of KPIP-LP 94.7 FM, a local radio station, which he manages to this day. Mary Beth Tinker pursued a career in medicine, working as a pediatric and emergency room nurse and a nurse practitioner. In 2013, Mary Beth left the nursing field and embarked on the “Tinker Tour,” where she travels the country telling her story and promoting civic education to young people.

    Industry observers note that clarence Brandenburg: Brandenburg v. Ohio.

    It has been revealed that let’s conclude with our least likable plaintiff, who nevertheless established one of the most enduring Supreme Court precedents. Clarence Brandenburg was born on March 3, 1916, in Lee County, Kentucky. A Marine Corps veteran, he worked at a General Electric plant and operated a television repair shop upon returning to civilian life. After declaring personal bankruptcy in 1959, Brandenburg began getting involved with white supremacist organizations and sought to become a leader of the KKK.

    In June 1964, Brandenburg spoke at a Klan rally, which was shown on a local television station. Brandenburg remarked “We're not a revengent organization, but if our President, our Congress, our Supreme Court, continues to suppress the white, Caucasian race, it's possible that there might have to be some revengeance taken. ... We are marching on Congress July the Fourth, four hundred thousand strong.” He was then charged with violating Ohio’s criminal syndicalism statute prohibiting advocating “sabotage, violence, or ... terrorism ... as a means of accomplishing ... political reform,” and later convicted.

    Recent findings suggest that brandenburg appealed, arguing that his speech was protected by the First Amendment. Specifically, he argued that Ohio could not punish him for advocating for unlawful action without showing that his speech was directed towards producing such action.

    Leonard Kirschner, arguing on behalf of Ohio at the Supreme Court, asserted that Brandenburg’s actions were not conducted in isolation and could lead to violence, contending that “the statements [made by Brandenburg] to 10 or 20 people can cause one heck of a lot of crime and violence and terrorism in any community. It only takes one person to cause it.”.

    The Supreme Court reversed Brandenburg’s conviction in 1969 on First Amendment grounds. According to the court, the Ohio statute in question failed to distinguish between an abstract endorsement of unlawful activity and speech directed towards producing imminent, lawless action. In doing so, the court established what became known as the Brandenburg test, which required that speech sufficient for incitement be “directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action” and “likely to incite or produce such action.”.

    It has been revealed that in 1971, Brandenburg was found guilty of harassing his Jewish neighbor by repeatedly calling him and uttering antisemitic slurs. He died on March 29, 1986.

    They came from different backgrounds, had very different worldviews, and dealt with different issues, but each of these plaintiffs had one thing in common: pushing up against the limits of state power. How that power manifested itself differed considerably, as did the court’s willingness to reign it in. For example, while the court has advanced a highly protective understanding of the First Amendment, it has been more hesitant to advance protections of economic liberty.

    Recent findings suggest that the nature of the plaintiff also mattered less in these cases than one might presume. Filburn was a farmer who grew wheat for his own personal consumption but did not prevail at the court. Brandenburg, on the other hand, expressed white supremacist ideas yet proved successful before the justices, becoming responsible for an entirely new free speech doctrine.

    Some may view the court blinding itself to the actual facts on the ground as too simplistic; others as an ideal to aspire to. On that note, we’ll give Justice Elena Kagan the final word: “the question is not do you like this party or do you like that party ... the question is what the law requires.”.

    Blake Fox is an intern for SCOTUSblog.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A judge had issued a "gag order," barring the media from reporting on what was noted in open court by the daughters of farming tycoon Michael Abatti.
    • (CN) â The Arizona Court of Appeals ruled Tuesday that news organizations can publish statements made, in open court, by the daughters of farming tycoon Michael Abatti, who is accused of shooting his estranged wife to death.
    • Sources indicate that “We are troubled that no one told the daughters the consequences of reading their statements in open court,” wrote Judge Jennifer Perkins in the unanimous opinion.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A judge had issued a "gag order," barring the media from reporting on what was noted in open court by the daughters of farming tycoon Michael Abatti.

    (CN) â The Arizona Court of Appeals ruled Tuesday that news organizations can publish statements made, in open court, by the daughters of farming tycoon Michael Abatti, who is accused of shooting his estranged wife to death.

    Sources indicate that “We are troubled that no one told the daughters the consequences of reading their statements in open court,” wrote Judge Jennifer Perkins in the unanimous opinion. “But once the daughters spoke in open court, the First Amendment protected the pressâs right to publish what they remarked, even if the failure to warn the daughters was inconsistent with the Victimsâ Bill of Rights.”.

    Abatti, a 63-year-old prominent farmer, is charged with first-degree murder in the death of his wife, 59-year-old Kerri Ann Abatti. The Imperial Valley couple had been embroiled in a bitter, three-year-long divorce, at the heart of which lay a $200 million trust. Arrested four weeks after the shooting, Abatti pleaded not guilty and is being held in custody, apparently unable to post the $5.5 million in bail.

    Sources indicate that at Abatti’s arraignment in December last year, his two daughters, who attended the hearing remotely, were allowed to read victim impact statements. A reporter from KPNX-TV Channel 12 was also listening to the proceedings remotely, with the court’s approval. The daughters’ statements were admitted into the record under seal, but they were also allowed to read them aloud during the hearing, which was open to the public. After the first statement was read, both the prosecutor and the defense attorney asked the court to glitch a “gag order,” barring members of the media from reporting what the daughters remarked.

    According to recent reports, KPNX objected to the gag order, arguing it was unconstitutional prior restraint. But both Abatti and his daughters urged the judge to stand by the order, Abatti arguing that publishing the statements would taint the small-town jury pool, and the daughters arguing they didn’t know the hearing was a public forum. The judge kept the gag order in place, and KPNX, joined by a handful of other local media outlets, filed a petition to overrule the order.

    The three-judge panel found the gag order was unconstitutional under both the Arizona and U.S. Constitutions.

    “A court may not bar the press from publishing what happens in open court unless the ‘gravity of the evil’ resulting from publication, ‘discounted by its improbability, justifies such invasion of free speech as is necessary to avoid the danger,’” Perkins wrote, citing a 1976 Supreme Court ruling.

    As to the argument that the daughters’ statements would taint the jury pool, Perkins wrote, “Even if the small, rural community here increases the risk of jury prejudice, that risk remains too speculative … Abatti has not shown, for example, that ordinary tools â a larger jury pool, questioning prospective jurors about media exposure, and instructing jurors to consider only the trial evidence â would fail to protect him from prejudice caused by reporting on his daughtersâ statements.”.

    The panel found that while the daughters might be harmed by the publicizing of their comments, “the gravity of the potential emotional harm to the adult daughters does not justify the prior restraint.”.

    Judges Jon Saline and Samuel Clark rounded out the panel.

    #192925. Breaking: Which justices favor the Trump administration the most (and least) on the emergency docket?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2002 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Which justices favor the Trump administration the most (and least) on the emergency docket?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When the Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s attempt to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook in June, the justices divided in a manner that would have been difficult to predict from some perceptions of the court.
    • In a recent development, four months later, the administration lost another emergency application, this time in a dispute over medical care for transgender federal prisoners.
    • In a recent development, the contrast points to a recurring theme of the Supreme Court’s emergency decisions: Although the conservative justices are often lumped together as “pro-Trump,” their rulings can depend on whether the dispute concerns immigration, presidential removal authority, federal spending, or the scope of emergency relief.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When the Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s attempt to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook in June, the justices divided in a manner that would have been difficult to predict from some perceptions of the court. Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Brett Kavanaugh joined Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson to leave Cook in office while the case proceeded. Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch, and Amy Coney Barrett dissented. The administration lost, but the court’s disagreement did not reflect the familiar ideological split.

    In a recent development, four months later, the administration lost another emergency application, this time in a dispute over medical care for transgender federal prisoners. In Trump v. Kingdom, Thomas and Alito indicated that they would have granted the requested stay, but no other justice publicly held that position. Unlike Trump v. Cook, which produced a signed opinion after oral argument, the Kingdom order disclosed nothing about the reasoning or votes behind the court’s denial.

    In a recent development, the contrast points to a recurring theme of the Supreme Court’s emergency decisions: Although the conservative justices are often lumped together as “pro-Trump,” their rulings can depend on whether the dispute concerns immigration, presidential removal authority, federal spending, or the scope of emergency relief. And whereas some justices have supported federal executive positions at broadly similar rates across presidencies, others appear far more likely to do so depending on whether the president is a Republican or Democrat.

    According to recent reports, the prior article in this series examined how frequently the Trump and Biden administrations prevailed. In turning to the individual justices, I reviewed federal executive-action decisions from 2017 through November 12, 2026, consolidated into 106 distinct substantive decisions. The three administrations account for 32, 36, and 38 decisions, respectively.

    There is a very vital qualification throughout: the court often publishes emergency orders without identifying each justice’s vote. The analysis thus assigned a justice to the court’s majority ruling when they were silent, absent an express position or other evidence indicating otherwise.

    So what can we say about the different justices’ support for the Trump administration on the emergency docket?

    Different presidents, different justices.

    The most consistent record belongs to Roberts. He aligned with federal executive positions in 23 of 31 eligible decisions during Trump’s first administration, 26 of 36 under Biden, and 28 of 38 during Trump’s second administration. Those figures amount to 74%, 72%, and 74%. The disputes changed markedly, but Roberts’ aggregate willingness to leave the federal government’s position intact – or grant it relief – barely moved. In other words, Roberts has typically supported executive power on the emergency docket regardless of who is president.

    The next most consistent justice, Barrett (though with a much lower sample size), aligned with Biden in 69% of her eligible decisions and Trump II in 78%. Third was Kavanaugh, with rates of 78%, 67%, and 79%. Then came Gorsuch, with rates of 83%, 54%, and 84%.

    In a recent development, thomas and Alito present a very different picture. Thomas supported the executive in 83% of eligible Trump I decisions, 39% under Biden, and 92% under Trump II. Alito’s corresponding figures were 83%, 47%, and 92%.

    According to recent reports, the liberal justices show the opposite movement, although their individual records differ. Kagan supported executive positions in 43% of eligible Trump I decisions, 94% under Biden, and 24% under Trump II. Sotomayor’s rates were 27%, 94%, and 16%. Jackson, who joined the court during Biden’s presidency, supported its executive position in 21 of 24 eligible decisions (88%), compared with three of 38 (8%) under Trump II.

    The figure above makes these distinctions particularly clear. Roberts remains between 72% and 74% across the three periods, while Thomas’ support moves from 83% under Trump I to 39% under Biden and 92% under Trump II. The middle group of Barrett, Kavanaugh, and Gorsuch is more varied, but each supported Biden’s executive position more frequently than a simple Republican-versus-Democratic framing might suggest.

    These numbers are telling, but they do not establish the reasons for why the justices decided as they did. For example, a president defending an environmental rule presents a very different legal glitch from one seeking permission to remove an independent agency official. To determine how much of the observed variation is associated with presidential identity, the next step is to examine the kinds of cases that produced it.

    The issues that unite and divide the justices.

    Immigration provides a useful point of comparison because it generated substantial emergency litigation under all three administrations. Roberts supported the executive in 10 of 11 immigration decisions under Trump I, three of six under Biden, and 11 of 13 under Trump II. Thomas supported the government in 10 of 10 eligible Trump I immigration decisions, two of six under Biden, and 12 of 13 under Trump II. Kagan’s comparable figures were six of eleven, six of six, and five of 13.

    Recent findings suggest that this is revealing. Roberts and Thomas both supported Trump’s immigration positions at high rates but not as much when Biden defended his administration’s policies. Kagan and Sotomayor supported Biden in all six coded immigration decisions, then opposed most of Trump II positions. But there is, of course, a key caveat: This category covers different immigration rules, as opposed to simple support for one president over another.

    Public-health and related health litigation under Biden revealed a sharper division within the conservative majority. In 10 eligible health-coded decisions, Roberts and Kavanaugh each supported the federal executive in seven, compared with one each for Thomas and Alito. Barrett supported it in five; Gorsuch in two. Kagan and Sotomayor each supported the government in nine such cases. (Jackson’s two favorable positions came from only three eligible decisions in this category, making her figure much less informative.).

    In a recent development, the court’s January 2022 vaccination decisions supply a concrete example. Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the liberals in allowing the administration to enforce a vaccination requirement for workers at healthcare facilities receiving Medicare or Medicaid funding, while Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett dissented. On the same day, Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the conservatives in blocking OSHA’s broader vaccination-or-testing standard. To Roberts and Kavanaugh, health litigation was clearly treated concern-by-issue.

    Let’s move on to personnel decisions, or the president’s control over the executive branch. In the nine Trump II personnel and removal decisions, Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett supported the executive in eight, while Roberts and Kavanaugh did so in seven. In four foreign-affairs and national-security decisions, Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch aligned with the government in all of these, compared with two for Roberts and Barrett.

    Subject matter therefore helps explain how things break down. The same conservative justice may support emergency intervention in a dispute over immigration enforcement while resisting it in a case involving agency regulation. The legal authority being asserted, the posture of the case, and the requested remedy all shape the decision.

    The coalitions inside the conservative majority.

    According to recent reports, so which justices most frequently aligned? At the front of the pack are Thomas and Alito, who agreed in all 38 coded Trump II decisions. Their alignment is particularly visible when the administration lost. In seven events, both of their positions favored more relief for the administration than the majority granted or would otherwise provide.

    According to recent reports, other pairings are almost as cohesive. Roberts and Barrett agreed in 35 of 36 Trump II decisions (97%). Roberts and Kavanaugh agreed in 36 of 38 of these (95%), as did Gorsuch and Kavanaugh. The next figure displays those pairings alongside the liberal and cross-ideological relationships. The high agreement rates show how often the conservatives arrive at the same apparent disposition, but the exceptions reveal competing views about the scope of emergency judicial intervention.

    The foreign-assistance dispute in Department of State v. AIDS Vaccine Advocacy Coalition, for instance, separated Roberts and Barrett from Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Kavanaugh. The four dissenters would have granted the administration relief from an order requiring payment for foreign-aid work already completed. Roberts and Barrett did not join that position. Their disagreement concerned what a district court could require of the government while the underlying funding litigation continued.

    A different alignment emerged in NIH v. American Public Health Association. There, the court granted partial relief in litigation over terminated research grants. Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Kavanaugh would have granted the administration’s request in full, while Roberts joined Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson in seeking to deny it altogether. Barrett supported an intermediate outcome.

    Sources indicate that in Cook, the division shifted again. Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the liberals in rejecting the administration’s attempt to immediately remove a Federal Reserve governor, while Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett dissented. In Trump v. Illinois, concerning the Trump administration’s deployment of National Guard forces, Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch disagreed with the court’s denial of relief to Trump, while Kavanaugh concurred in the judgment on narrower grounds.

    It has been revealed that the evidence points toward distinctive approaches to removal authority, spending, the judicial supervision of agencies, and emergency remedies. Justices who agree in one field can diverge in another, and partial orders sometimes put a justice between two groups seeking opposing forms of relief.

    The liberal justices and the unusual alliances across ideological lines.

    The three liberal justices also exhibited some meaningful disagreements. Under Trump II, Jackson aligned with the executive in only three of 38 emergency decisions (8%), compared with six for Sotomayor (16%) and nine for Kagan (24%). Kagan and Sotomayor agreed in 35 of 38 such decisions; Kagan and Jackson in 32. The differences are not as dramatic as those dividing the conservatives, but they complicate the assumption that the liberal trio behaves as a single bloc in every emergency dispute.

    It has been revealed that their publicly registered dissents differ as well. Jackson expressly opposed a Trump II executive position in 26 decisions, Sotomayor in 23, and Kagan in 20. In FCC v. Brown, for example, Sotomayor and Jackson publicly indicated that they would deny the agency’s stay application, while Kagan registered no public disagreement.

    Trump’s second term has produced more than one identifiable cross-ideological alignment. The five-justice majority in Cook included Roberts, Kavanaugh, and the three liberals, while the NIH grants dispute placed Roberts and the liberals together against complete relief. Barrett also joined certain portions of Sotomayor’s dissent in Trump v. J.G.G., a dispute involving the Alien Enemies Act, although her partial join should not necessarily be counted as agreement with the liberals on the case.

    It has been revealed that these examples again highlight why the distinction between shared results and shared legal reasoning is crucial. A justice can favor the same outcome as an ideological opponent while arriving there for entirely different reasons (we see this with concurrences in merits cases all the time). Separate opinions can also reveal agreement on a particular procedural or statutory question even when the justices disagree on the ultimate relief. At the same time, the emergency docket makes these relationships especially difficult to measure comprehensively because many orders contain no individual vote information at all.

    My analysis of the emergency docket demonstrates a chief most reluctant to favor one administration over another, with Barrett and Kavanaugh following closely behind; Gorsuch acting more favorably towards the Trump administration, although not overwhelmingly so; Thomas and Alito disproportionately favoring Trump over Biden; and the three liberal justices acting as a near mirror image of Thomas and Alito – although to varied degrees.

    We thus see a conservative majority whose members separate over particular exercises of federal power, a liberal bloc with distinguishable voting and dissent records, and occasional alliances that cross ideological lines.

    Dr. Adam Feldman is the creator and author of the blog Empirical SCOTUS and the Substack Legalytics.

    #192922. Tech Report: Refugees, asylum, and Supreme Court exceptionalism

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2108 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Refugees, asylum, and Supreme Court exceptionalism

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2108 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American exceptionalism, the idea that the United States is uniquely virtuous, has deep roots that predate the nation itself.
    • In a recent development, at best, American exceptionalism can be beneficent in intent and beneficial in result.
    • And then there is the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American exceptionalism, the idea that the United States is uniquely virtuous, has deep roots that predate the nation itself. The founders of New England, in words echoed by President Ronald Reagan, famously declared that it was to be “as a citty upon a Hill. The eies of all people are upon us.”.

    In a recent development, at best, American exceptionalism can be beneficent in intent and beneficial in result. In time the Upcoming England states would become leaders in the abolition of slavery. Closer to our time, the United States would translate its victory in the Second Word War into the Marshall Plan, the World Bank, and the currently embattled international legal order under the aegis of the United Nations. The 18th Amendment, the juvenile death penalty (until 2005), and the failure to guarantee a right to healthcare furnish examples of exceptionalism gone wrong.

    And then there is the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law. At the Founding and for decades thereafter, the court tended to embrace “the law of nations,” either as a guide to interpreting relevant statutes or even as furnishing a rule of decision in appropriate circumstances. In more recent times, however, majorities have balked at viewing treaties as self-executing, taking guidance from the International Court of Justice, or applying statutes that expressly incorporate “the law of nations” into domestic law.

    Recent findings suggest that A grant of certiorari just this month will likely confirm the trend. The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, in which the justices will review one of the Trump administration’s earliest attempts to restrict immigration. On the administration’s first day, a presidential proclamation declared that “an invasion is ongoing on the southern border.” The proclamation, among other things, sought to suspend entry to the United States for non-citizens “engaged in the invasion,” even for refugees fleeing persecution and seeking to apply for asylum. But the edict went one step further. It also mandated expedited removal to asylum seekers who had crossed the border seeking to apply for asylum and provided for expedited removal of such persons.

    The proclamation was issued notwithstanding a congressional framework that seeks to facilitate asylum – indefinite lawful residence – to those escaping persecution in their home country, set forth primarily in the 1952 Immigration and Nationality Act as amended by the 1980 Refugee Act and later amendments (codified under Title 8 of the U.S. Code). This framework: a) ensures a right to apply for asylum, b) links eligibility for asylum to refugee status, and c) provides protections against the government removing persons who would be likely to face persecution or torture.

    Section 1158 establishes the right to seek asylum. It provides that “[a]ny alien who is physically present in the United States … irrespective of such alien’s status, may apply for asylum.” The same section makes eligibility for asylum conditional, among other things, on a demonstration of refugee status. For this the statute relies on the definition of refugee in section 1101(a)(42) as a person who is unwilling or unable to return to their home country “because of persecution or a well-founded fear of persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in turn, safeguards from removal come from two sources. The immigration statute itself states that noncitizens cannot be removed to a country where the attorney general determines that the “alien’s life or freedom would be threatened in that country because of the alien’s race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.” In addition, the Foreign Affairs Reform & Restructuring Act of 1998 restricts removal to a country when “there are substantial grounds for believing the person would be in danger of being subjected to torture.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the Trump administration initially justified the denial of asylum and removal protections to those within the United States by invoking the president’s authority to suspend entry “of any aliens or of any class of aliens into the United States [that] would be detrimental to the interests of the United States.” The logic is that no one who violated the suspension by entering should be entitled to asylum and removal protections. To this defense the administration has added the formal role of the attorney general and director of Homeland Security. The INA grants each official the authority to grant asylum to eligible applicants as well as withhold removal for those who qualify. At the same time, the statute makes clear that these decisions are subject to individualized judicial review under an “abuse of discretion” standard. (At least until the second Trump administration, decisions not to grant relief to those who had demonstrated that they had qualified for asylum were the “exceedingly rare“ exception.).

    The lower courts rejected both justifications. Judge Randolph Moss of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia dismissed the administration’s claim that the president’s suspension of entry to those “engaged in [the] invasion” invalidated asylum and removal protections that expressly applied to persons physically in the country. The D.C. Circuit agreed with a slightly different emphasis. Writing for the majority, Judge Michelle Childs also rejected the idea that a suspension of entry justified eliminating asylum and removal safeguards for those present in the United States. To this point she added that, as a grant of asylum is discretionary, the express right to apply it entails individualized consideration rather than blanket elimination. (Judge Justin Walker issued a partial dissenting argument that the grant of discretionary authority permits a blanket denial of asylum claims.).

    The D.C. courts’ holdings are not wrong so far as they go. Suspending entry would appear to be a different power from removing someone after they had entered. The provisions for asylum strongly imply individualized consideration and even suggest a presumption of granting asylum to those who meet the detailed eligibility requirements. The relevant provisions plainly bar removal of those who qualify for that protection. But whether this reasoning will be sufficient at the Supreme Court is another matter. This is so not least given the justices’ recent penchant for giving the executive wide latitude on immigration.

    But the justices should take into account some additional perspective.

    One relevant perspective comes from international law. Surprising as it may seem, the United States is not exceptional in having to grapple with immigration, refugees, and asylum. More surprising still, these common global challenges has yielded what should be familiar, common legal standards that apply, and to a great extent which owe their development to, the United States. Perhaps most surprising of all, standard domestic doctrines invite reference to this body of law when interpreting applicable federal statutes.

    According to recent reports, consider first asylum. As an initial matter, the domestic asylum framework incorporates international standards as a function of congressional intent. As the court itself recognized in 1987’s INS v. Cardozo-Fonseca, Congress enacted the Refugee Act of 1980 to bring U.S. law in conformity with the nation’s obligations as a state party to the 1967 Protocol to the 1951 Refugee Convention. Crucially, in determining those obligations, the court sensibly drew upon the views of the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Refugees.

    It has been revealed that what do those obligations contemplate? The Refugee Conventions do not expressly provide for a right to apply for long-term asylum, as opposed to specifying rights for refugees fleeing persecution. But the UNCHR has maintained that international law presupposes individualized consideration of refugee status, especially before that status is denied. Given that Congress made the requirements for refugee status the basis for being eligible for asylum, it would be odd to conclude that the U.S. would remain in conformity with the convention as interpreted by the UN’s most authoritative body should the executive reject the right to seek asylum by means of a categorial denial of all asylum claims.

    Recent findings suggest that not surprisingly, categorical rejection of asylum claims would also be at variance with widespread international practice, especially as mandated in Europe. And neither last nor least, the administration’s position would also be inconsistent with the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights’ express guarantee of a right to asylum. Though not binding, the UDHR was adopted without dissent by the UN General Assembly, reflects the dominant position of the Member States, and informs their practice.

    The Charming Betsy canon leads to the same conclusion. In the 1804 case Murray v. the Schooner Charming Betsy, Chief Justice John Marshall famously stated that “an act of Congress ought never to be construed to violate the law of nations if any other possible construction remains.” Marshall’s reference to the “law of nations” is generally understood to apply to modern customary international law. International custom arises given a near consensus of state practice perused out of a sense of legal obligation.

    Section 1158’s grant of authority to the executive to grant asylum applications can be construed at least in two ways. It might mean a complete categorical discretion to deny. Or it might be better understood to assume individualized consideration. The latter clearly better comports with international practice. Yet there is even a stronger consideration. Customary, and for that matter treaty law, clearly prohibits removal to countries where a refugee has a well-founded fear of facing persecution or torture. When the result is expedited removal, the categorical denial of asylum status to persons claiming to escape from persecution and torture places the U.S. in obvious jeopardy of violating exactly this well-established international prohibition.

    According to recent reports, which brings up the matter of removal itself. Here the upshot of Congress’ intent is more direct. Article 33.1 of the 1951 Refugee Convention provides: “No Contracting State shall expel or return (“refouler”) a refugee in any manner whatsoever to the frontiers of territories where his life or freedom would be threatened on account of his race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion.” Likewise, Article 3.1 of the Convention Against Torture mandates that “No State Party shall expel, return ("refouler") or extradite a person to another State where there are substantial grounds for believing that he would be in danger of being subjected to torture.” As noted, the Refugee Act in the first instance sought to place the U.S. in conformity with the Refugee Convention. FARRA sought to do the same with CAT. Categorically removing persons in the U.S. seeking asylum all but guarantees violations of the treaties that Congress sought to uphold.

    In a recent development, so strong is the congressional intent argument that the Charming Betsy need not set sail. Yet even if the relevant statutory provisions were somehow ambiguous, the Charming Betsy canon would compel rejection of the administration’s position. Assume that section 1182(f), which grants the executive discretion to deny asylum claims, authorizes a categorial denial of applications across the board. Assume further that this section, along with section 1185(a)(1), can be read to permit removal of persons within the United States denied the opportunity to apply for asylum on the basis of persecution or torture. Even without the conventions, international practice has separately established “non-refoulement” – the prohibition of returning, or “refouling,” a person to return to a territory where he may be exposed to persecution as a matter of binding customary international law. Reading the relevant statutes to permit removal would then constitute a clear violation of non-refoulement. That reading would therefore also run counter to the Charming Betsy canon.

    A sad yet likely irony is that Mullin v. RAICES will privilege one strand of American exceptionalism over another. Much of the international law relevant to the case reflects the nation’s exceptional effort to leverage its dominance after the Second World War not to establish a traditional empire, but to construct a rules-based international order. One of many achievements was the 1951 Refugee Convention, like the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, brought about in no small part thanks to the efforts of Eleanor Roosevelt as a U.S. representative to the UN. Against this is the view that America has little to heed from the rest of the world, including on matters that implicate international affairs. The court adopted this stance on immigration as recently as last term. We shall see which view prevails.

    Martin Flaherty is Charles and Marie Robertson Visiting Professor at the School of Public and International Affairs at Princeton, and Leitner Family Professor Chair of International Human Rights Law at Fordham Law School in Newly introduced York.
